items.summary:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 22 – The Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) has deployed a search and rescue helicopter alongside drones as the operation to locate an elderly man who went missing while hiking in Aberdare National Park enters its next phase.
In an update on Sunday, KWS said the search for Elder David K
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 22 – The Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) has deployed a search and rescue helicopter alongside drones as the operation to locate an elderly man who went missing while hiking in Aberdare National Park enters its next phase.
In an update on Sunday, KWS said the search for Elder David Kenneth Kihuna, who disappeared on Saturday was still underway, with multi-agency teams conducting extensive searches across the park’s challenging terrain.
The agency said the operation involves KWS rangers, the Mountain Rescue Team from Mount Kenya National Park, local community guides and other supporting partners.
The deployment of aerial surveillance equipment is intended to help rescue teams cover more ground and navigate areas obscured by the park’s dense forest canopy.
“Our thoughts and prayers are with his family and loved ones as we work through this difficult period together,” KWS stated.
The wildlife agency commended the rescue teams for their dedication, noting that personnel were working around the clock to locate the missing hiker.
KWS reaffirmed its commitment to the operation, saying it was utilising every available resource to bring Kihuna home safely.
The agency added that further updates would be issued as the search and rescue operation progresses.

items.summary:
Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua have a genuine animosity, says Olympic gold medallist Audley Harrison | 'We need to see it'
Audley Harrison doesn't believe Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua has been left too late in their careers; "they're not in their primes but there's still enough there and the animosit
items.text:
Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua have a genuine animosity, says Olympic gold medallist Audley Harrison | 'We need to see it'
Audley Harrison doesn't believe Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua has been left too late in their careers; "they're not in their primes but there's still enough there and the animosity that they have is genuine. So it's a fight definitely I want to see," the Olympic gold medallist said
Sunday 22 November 2026 08:43, UK
Audley Harrison has backed Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury to deliver when they fight on December 11 in Cardiff.
Harrison was one half of an all-British heavyweight grudge match when he boxed David Haye in a 2010 event that was much hyped but ultimately disappointed.
Harrison though doesn't think Fury and Joshua have left their fight too late.
"'Politricks' has always been there in boxing, always unfortunately messing up boxing," Harrison told Sky Sports.
"I will be sitting on the edge of my seat for Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua. They're not in their primes but there's still enough there and the animosity that they have is genuine. So it's a fight definitely I want to see. While it's a little late, I can't argue with that.
"It's not going to be them in their primes but it's going to be good enough. We need to see it for sure."
He added: "Look at Mike Tyson-Lennox Lewis, everyone was complaining for that fight, that fight was like five years too late in many people's eyes.
"I was there in Memphis, it was a great fight, great atmosphere, exactly what we wanted.
"Lennox banged him out but the fight was so exciting."
Harrison preceded Joshua as an Olympic super-heavyweight gold medallist for Great Britain. But he did not scale the heights Joshua achieved in the professional ranks. Joshua has twice been a unified heavyweight world champion and has made a habit of selling out stadium shows in London and Cardiff.
"All of these guys came from nowhere. AJ went to the Olympics not as the favourite, same as Deontay Wilder, and they punched their way to glory," Harrison said.
"When Joshua turned pro he was raw as hell, you've got to give him credit he was able to go through.
"When he lost to [Andy] Ruiz they crucified him because he was meant to win, but he was still raw. He's always been really disciplined, he's strong and he's always come into the ring ready.
"Technically and tactically he's been off in some fights, obviously with [Oleksandr] Usyk, obviously with [Daniel] Dubois. But came back in the [Wladimir] Klitschko fight. When you look at his career, you've got to take your hat off. He wasn't perfect, but he's not supposed to be."
Harrison added: "He's still got the power, he's still got the punch but he doesn't have the punch resistance now.
"We're seeing that with Joshua, we're seeing that with Fury. We haven't seen that with Usyk yet. I haven't seen him start to flounder yet in terms of punch resistance.
"To be fair to AJ and Tyson Fury, they've both had a legendary career, when you look at what they've done, not just the money they've made, if you look at their legacy."

items.title: Why Somalia’s president turned against his former ally, the UAE
items.summary:
Why Somalia’s president turned against his former ally, the UAE
Behind Somalia’s break with the UAE lies a domestic power struggle with regional leaders close to Abu Dhabi.
Three years ago, at a town hall meeting in Mogadishu, Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud defended one of his country’s most
items.text:
Why Somalia’s president turned against his former ally, the UAE
Behind Somalia’s break with the UAE lies a domestic power struggle with regional leaders close to Abu Dhabi.
Three years ago, at a town hall meeting in Mogadishu, Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud defended one of his country’s most controversial foreign partnerships.
The United Arab Emirates, he declared, was “one of the greatest pillars” of Somalia’s war against the al-Qaeda-linked armed group al-Shabab. He praised Abu Dhabi’s support for the country’s armed forces despite longstanding concerns about its political influence.
Having returned to power in 2022, Mohamud sought to repair relations with the Gulf state after a period of strained ties under his predecessor, while reassuring a sceptical Somali public that the UAE’s involvement was a boon rather than a hindrance.
This year, that relationship unravelled spectacularly.
On November 19, Somalia ordered the Emirati ambassador to leave the country and recalled its own envoy from Abu Dhabi, marking the sharpest rupture yet in a relationship that had shifted from close security cooperation and deep commercial ties to open hostility.
The UAE said it had already withdrawn its diplomatic staff from Mogadishu in January.
The decision came 10 months after Somalia annulled several commercial, defence and security agreements with the UAE, accusing its former ally of undermining its sovereignty.
In a sharp public rebuke two days before the expulsion order, Mohamud accused the UAE of heightening political divisions, financing rival regional administrations and supporting armed actors operating beyond the federal government’s control.
“A brother does not burn your house. A brother does not buy your property without your knowledge. A brother does not divide your family,” he said.
“After years of diplomatic engagement, the Federal Government assesses that UAE policies threaten Somalia’s national security,” Awes Hagi Yusuf Ahmed, Somalia’s national security adviser (NSA), said in a post on X.
The UAE hit back, accusing Mogadishu of allowing its internal political disputes to strain bilateral ties, in an apparent reference to the president’s contentious relations with some of Somalia’s semi-autonomous regional administrations, which maintain close ties with Abu Dhabi.
Anwar Gargash, a senior Emirati official, said the UAE’s ties with Somalia would “remain deeper and stronger” despite the president’s criticism.
The diplomatic rupture comes amid an escalating domestic power struggle between Mohamud and regional leaders resisting his efforts to reassert federal authority, several of whom have cultivated close ties with Abu Dhabi.
It also marks a striking reversal for a president during whose first term the UAE significantly expanded its foothold in Somalia and who later emerged as one of Abu Dhabi’s strongest defenders.
Somalia divided
Somalia’s efforts to rebuild national institutions since the establishment of a permanent federal government in 2012 have unfolded alongside the consolidation of regional administrations that retain considerable autonomy and political power.
Abu Dhabi’s ties with Mogadishu deepened during Mohamud’s first presidency, from 2012 to 2017.
The UAE reopened its embassy in the capital in 2014, and Mohamud inaugurated a UAE-funded military training centre for Somali forces the following year.
At the same time, the Gulf state cultivated commercial, security and diplomatic ties with regional administrations, including Puntland and Jubbaland, as well as Somaliland, which declared independence from Somalia in 1991.
The UAE is also one of Somalia’s most important trading partners, serving as an important source of imports and a hub for Somali businesses trading in international markets.
But its influence extends well beyond trade, with big investments in infrastructure and security concentrated in Somaliland, Puntland and Jubbaland.
Among the most visible of these investments is Berbera port in Somaliland, where Dubai’s state-owned port operator DP World has invested heavily in expanding the facility and developing a trade corridor connecting it to Ethiopia and the wider region.
Through its subsidiary P&O Ports, the company also operates Bosaso port in Puntland, with both ports providing crucial sources of revenue for their respective administrations.
Somaliland’s Foreign Minister Abdirahman Dahir Adam said the UAE treated it as an independent state, making it an attractive partner, while Emirati investments had created jobs and improved regional connectivity.
“The UAE saw Somaliland’s potential early and backed that view with real investment,” Adam told Al Jazeera.
“The impact on our economy has been significant. DP World’s development of Berbera Port and the Berbera Corridor has turned Berbera into a serious regional gateway,” he added.
Their strategic location along the Gulf of Aden also gives Somaliland and Puntland considerable leverage, making them attractive partners for foreign powers seeking a foothold along one of the world’s busiest shipping routes.
The UAE has developed military facilities near both ports, while in Puntland it helped establish and fund the Puntland Maritime Police Force (PMPF), initially an antipiracy unit that has since become an important counterterrorism force.
More recently, it has supported Puntland’s campaign against ISIL (ISIS) in Somalia with drone attacks and carried out a strike this year against al-Shabab in support of Puntland’s forces, a security official in the region told Al Jazeera.
Abu Dhabi maintains similar commercial and security ties with Jubbaland, which borders Kenya, although the extent of its involvement there is less publicly documented.
A senior Puntland official speaking anonymously told Al Jazeera the UAE’s interventions had helped regional states consolidate their authority, with no equivalent assistance coming from the federal government. “It is obvious why on that level the UAE is a more important partner,”

items.title: The European revolt may be coming to the UK
items.summary:
The European revolt may be coming to the UK
There is enough justified anger among the British youth to spark a wave of mass protests.
The protests engulfing Europe represent a new level of popular mobilisation quite unlike any historical precedent. In France, Spain, Italy, Serbia, Germany and other
items.text:
The European revolt may be coming to the UK
There is enough justified anger among the British youth to spark a wave of mass protests.
The protests engulfing Europe represent a new level of popular mobilisation quite unlike any historical precedent. In France, Spain, Italy, Serbia, Germany and other countries across the continent, mass movements are challenging austerity and government failures.
On Friday, the United Kingdom saw what is likely to be the beginning of its own wave of youth-driven demonstrations. Thousands of students walked out of hundreds of schools and universities around the country, from Aberdeen to Brighton, Swansea to Nottingham, making it one of the largest student mobilisations since the tripling of tuition fees back in 2010.
The protests were called by organisations involved in the International Conference Against War, a pan-European initiative aimed at coordinating the movements against militarism. The University and College Union (UCU) was the first union to back the initiative with a National Day of Action, urging members across the university sector to hold protests and rallies alongside students.
That major unions followed UCU in supporting the walkouts, including Unison, Unite, the National Education Union (NEU), GMB and the Educational Institute of Scotland (EIS), speaks to the potential of union support.
In London, demonstrations from universities and colleges converged on Trafalgar Square to chants of “fight for our future, not their wars” before moving to Downing Street to hear student activists and trade union leaders berate the government for prioritising defence spending over education and public services.
There is indeed much for British youth to be angry about. Like in the rest of Europe, young people in the UK are facing a convergence of high inflation, unemployment, economic stagnation, the gutting of public services and deteriorating living standards, including a housing crisis stoked by property speculation. Combined with police brutality over solidarity with Palestine, unrestrained racism and sexism and expectations of environmental and climate catastrophe, mass protest is rather predictable.
According to government estimates, close to one million people between 16 and 24 years of age are “Neets” – not in education, employment or training; this is more than 13 percent of that age group. Young people make up more than 40 percent of the unemployed in the country. Apart from a tough job market, there is also a rampant mental health epidemic and an education system that few can afford.
Here we have the makings of a social and economic crisis waiting to happen, and yet the government response has been to seek more austerity.
It is a wonder that Alan Milburn, former Labour minister responsible for introducing private finance into the NHS in the late 1990s, was commissioned to write the controversial report on Neets for the government. Why bother to provide welfare when the private sector can solve the crisis? Unsurprisingly, Milburn’s recommendations are market-focused and include cutting certain benefits for youth, including for those with disabilities.
This comes on top of years of austerity in the higher education sector. Job cuts and course closures have become standard responses from university managements dealing with the lack of direct government funding. Many describe it as academic vandalism. What funding cuts have produced is extreme dysfunction, chaos and mismanagement: Faustian bargains with banks, management consultants and corporate outsourcing that serve efficiency and profit over quality provision.
While education and civilian job openings are dwindling, British youth are offered more opportunities in the army, which is now promoting a fully paid 18-month “foundation scheme”.
Military training, bolstered by a public campaign around “warfighting readiness” as part of last year’s Strategic Defence Review, was the brainchild of ministers under Keir Starmer, one of the most unpopular prime ministers in British history. True to form, Starmer pushed through an additional 15 billion pounds ($19.6bn) towards defence immediately before leaving office, for a total of 298 billion pounds ($389.8bn) over four years.
This is a worrying trend across Europe: While there are diminishing funds for public services, military spending is shooting up. This fact has not been lost on young people.
But what is driving this rearmament frenzy is that the European project is increasingly being bound together by NATO, along with Trump’s insistence that the EU should pay its fair share in maintaining the alliance. Support for Ukraine against Russia is at the centre of that project.
If youth mobilisation in the UK reaches the same level as in France, for example, this could be the first major test of Andy Burnham’s government. The French revolt was started over education – not the first strikes in French history over education, considering the origins of the 1968 uprisings. Still, France spends 5.1 percent of GDP on education.
The UK spends 4.1 percent of GDP on education, and even part of this budget has been diverted to defence, with less funding for schools in the coming years.
The UK has had seven prime ministers in the past decade, each one unable to deliver desperately needed income and wealth redistribution. A decade of Tory prime ministers allowed the rich to get very rich. Starmer continued the tradition. He was hammered by Reform and the Greens in the last local elections, firstly because he was unable to come through on the social democratic promises that many were hoping a Labour government would provide.
But second, he failed to recognise the genuine anger over British complicity in the Palestinian genocide, and then responded to mass protest with punitive legislation. Notwithstanding the Burnham bounce, the sitting prime minister has stuck to the same tack as his predecessor. His new foreign secretary has admitted that the government got it wrong over

Kansas City Current have defeated the Washington Spirit in a closely-contested final to be crowned the NW
items.text:
Kansas City Current defeat Washington Spirit 2-1 to lift first NWSL title
Trinity Rodman left in tears after scoring Spirit’s only goal as DiBernardo and Debinha give Current closely-fought win.
Kansas City Current have defeated the Washington Spirit in a closely-contested final to be crowned the NWSL champions for the first time as Trinity Rodman’s bid to avoid a third consecutive final defeat ended in bitter disappointment in Washington, DC.
Vanessa DiBernardo curled in a goal direct from a corner and Brazilian international Debinha added a second in stoppage time to set up Kansas City’s 2-1 victory at Audi Field on Saturday.
Rodman headed in a 98th-minute goal to pull one back for Spirit, but Kansas City held on to win.
“We knew it was going to be a battle; we felt good coming out of the first half,” said DiBernardo, who was named the championship MVP months after returning to professional football following the birth of her daughter.
“We just had to be patient and finish off the game.”
It was another crushing loss for United States star Rodman and her Spirit teammates, who were also beaten in the final in 2025 and 2024.
Rodman, who was in tears at the final whistle, was knocked out of her stride earlier in the game.
The 24-year-old was on the receiving end of a rugged aerial challenge from Kansas City’s Laney Rouse after just five minutes and needed treatment on the sidelines.
Rodman returned to the field grimacing in pain and clutching her shoulder but completed the game.
The opening goal came early in the second half, with DiBernardo’s in-swinging corner looping into the net after Kansas City’s Kayla Sharples cleverly blocked Washington goalkeeper Sandy MacIver.
Deep in stoppage time, Debinha added Current’s second after a sweeping counterattack, before Rodman’s header was too little, too late.
The victory was Kansas City’s first NWSL title after losing in the championship game to the Portland Thorns in 2022.

items.title: What Sandpapergate reveals about Australian cricket
items.summary:
What Sandpapergate reveals about Australian cricket
A toxic culture of winning at any cost has been hiding behind the myth of ‘mateship’.
“I knew it was wrong. I knew that using sandpaper was not simply pushing the boundaries of the laws of cricket. It was cheating,” former Australian Test cricketer
items.text:
What Sandpapergate reveals about Australian cricket
A toxic culture of winning at any cost has been hiding behind the myth of ‘mateship’.
“I knew it was wrong. I knew that using sandpaper was not simply pushing the boundaries of the laws of cricket. It was cheating,” former Australian Test cricketer Cameron Bancroft wrote in a 4,000-word expose.
His frank admission that he knowingly cheated and then lied to investigators and the Australian public was raw.
The footage of Bancroft shoving sandpaper down the front of his trousers, in an attempt to hide his illegal ball tampering during the 2018 Test series between South Africa and Australia, has been seen all over the world; the act of cheating has never been in question.
But the fallout, eight years in the making, no longer centres on a square of sandpaper. It revolves around a culture that placed winning above sound ethics. It created such deep-seated fear that lying – both directly and by omission – became a means to survive, and ultimately exposed the national belief that Australian men’s cricket was underpinned by a sacred sense of “mateship” – standing above self-interest – as a myth.
The basic facts of Australia’s ball-tampering scandal have long been established. Bancroft, with the tacit encouragement of teammate David Warner and under then-captain Steve Smith, who elected to look the other way, executed a premeditated plan to alter the ball’s surface during the third Test in Cape Town, in order to promote reverse swing.
Once he was caught, the public outrage and revulsion were overwhelming. Cricket Australia, the national cricket governing body, rushed through an inadequate investigation, omitting many of the touring party, and concluding that knowledge of the plan was confined to Bancroft, Warner and Smith. It imposed draconian penalties: yearlong bans for Smith and Warner, nine months for Bancroft.
Coach Darren Lehmann eventually stood down, followed out the door by several support staff, administrators and board members.
The cone of silence surrounding the affair cracked open with the release of Usman Khawaja’s autobiography, Sabr, in which he alleged everyone in the dressing room was in on the plan. Players and coaching staff came out publicly to either back Khawaja’s story or reject his version of events.
Current team captain Pat Cummins, who was also part of the team in 2018, publicly insisted that he did not know about the use of sandpaper. This was reportedly the final straw for Bancroft: “It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone,” he wrote.
For eight years he had borne the brunt of being labelled a cheat and watched his former teammates carry on with their Test careers – including Smith and Warner, after serving their bans.
Within hours of Cricket Australia’s announcement of an independent “truth forum” that would provide a “safe place” for discussion – a belated effort to stem the tide of damaging public confessions – Bancroft’s self-penned expose was published in The West Australian newspaper.
Not only did he insist that everyone was in on the scheme, but it was not an isolated occurrence, as the investigation had concluded; he had also used sandpaper in the second Test in Gqeberha that year.
“I made a terrible decision because I wanted to belong in the Australian team,” Bancroft wrote.
The context of his choice shouldn’t be overlooked. He was a 24-year-old adult, yet a junior member of the side playing in his seventh Test, and he desperately wanted to fit in.
The years leading up to the South Africa tour were defined by an increasingly toxic culture in which the boundaries of sportsmanship were tested, stretched and treated as pliable when convenient.
The Australian men’s team were the self-appointed guardians of “the line”, their own behaviour consistently justified as being on the right side of what was acceptable under the mantra of playing “hard but fair”. There was a lack of strong and ethical leadership in the dressing room, from the coaching staff all the way up to the Cricket Australia boardroom.
An independent, wide-ranging review by ethics nonprofit organisation The Ethics Centre, conducted in the aftermath of the affair, exposed a culture of “winning without counting the costs” that seeped throughout Cricket Australia. It was a culture in which staff and players feared the consequences of speaking honestly. It is no wonder that silence and dishonesty flourished in order to protect the brand and ensure self-preservation.
“We were frightened,” Bancroft wrote. “We were under pressure. We were trying to manage a situation that was rapidly getting away from us.”
While the on-field reputation of the Australian Test team has improved since 2018, fronted by captains Tim Paine and then Cummins, the blackened seeds sown were nourished by years of resentment and grievance, and have now emerged fully grown in blighted and twisted ugliness.
The complexity and nuance of ball-tampering have been overtaken by accusations of who knew what and a tug-of-war over who owns the truth – not to mention an administration that desperately hoped a web of half-truths and omissions would hold.
It has held a confronting mirror to the wider public’s veneration of “mateship”, the close bond of brotherhood that Australians have long held as core to their national identity. The baggy green cap worn by the country’s Test cricketers has been its unofficial symbol. Friendship may be universal, but mateship – that’s unique to Australia. The cap looks increasingly frayed with every public disclosure.
For Australians to accept that a young player would consider cheating, and then lie about cheating, as the best way of fitting in with his “mates”, it would mean questioning this idea of national exceptionalism. It would mean accepting that self-interest would trump the sacrosanct bonds of selfless “mateship”.
There have been widespread calls for Australian cricket to move on and a growing collective weariness that this unseemly and unflattering saga

items.title: Ledama defends shooting threat, blames political rivals over auction drama
items.summary: NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 22 – Narok Senator Ledama Olekina has defended his threat to shoot individuals captured in a viral confrontation, insisting that the incident involved alleged auctioneers who had trespassed onto private property to execute a court order over a former Senate employee’s compensation
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 22 – Narok Senator Ledama Olekina has defended his threat to shoot individuals captured in a viral confrontation, insisting that the incident involved alleged auctioneers who had trespassed onto private property to execute a court order over a former Senate employee’s compensation dispute.
Olekina dismissed reports that auctioneers had moved to repossess his personal vehicle, saying the individuals had instead seized the keys to a delivery truck belonging to a private company in which he is a shareholder.
In a statement issued on Saturday, November 21, the senator accused political opponents and social media platforms of distorting the incident, claiming the footage was being exploited to damage his reputation.
The controversy erupted after a video circulated online showing Olekina in a heated exchange with a group of men near a vehicle, during which he was heard threatening to shoot one of them.
“Nitakupiga risasi kichwa,” the senator is heard telling one of the individuals in the footage.
Olekina defended his remarks, describing the individuals as “goons” whom he accused of harassing his driver during an attempted property attachment.
He maintained that he would not allow anyone to trespass onto his property and warned that those who attempted to do so would face consequences.
In his statement, the senator traced the dispute to 2017, when a Senate staff member assigned to his office was dismissed for allegedly absconding from duty.
He said the former employee, identified as Rotiken, subsequently pursued a claim of unfair termination, resulting in Labour Court orders authorising the attachment of property.
Olekina questioned why he was being held personally responsible for an employment dispute involving a constitutional institution, arguing that the Senate’s staff obligations are funded through the Parliamentary Service Commission (PSC) and not individual senators.
“Let me be clear: the Senate of the Republic of Kenya is a constitutional institution, not Ledama Olekina’s private estate. Staff salaries and employment obligations are funded by the public purse through the Parliamentary Service Commission, not from an individual Senator’s pocket,” he said.
He further claimed that the individuals entered the premises of a private company in which he holds shares and seized the keys to a delivery truck, alleging they were seeking to recover Sh365,000 over the former employee’s claim.
“No personal vehicle of mine was ever under auction,” he said.
The senator questioned the legal basis for attaching assets belonging to a private company over an employment dispute involving a public institution, arguing that institutional liabilities should not automatically be transferred to individual officeholders or separate business entities.
Court dispute
However, the dispute has a longer legal history than the senator’s latest statement suggests.The former employee, Zakayo Rotiken, served as a Narok North Constituency Coordinator between 2017 and 2020 before his dismissal.
The Employment and Labour Relations Court reportedly ruled in Rotiken’s favour on October 31, 2023, over his dismissal and unpaid salary arrears. The decision was subsequently upheld on appeal, with the outstanding decree, including accrued interest, reported to have risen to approximately Sh1.2 million.
Reports indicate that the auctioneers were acting on court-backed warrants to recover the outstanding amount.
Rotiken’s legal team condemned the senator’s threats, arguing that the former employee had pursued his claim through the judicial system and should not face intimidation for seeking enforcement of a court decision.
Rotiken maintained that he had been unfairly dismissed and was entitled to the compensation awarded through the court process. He called on security agencies to protect officers executing their lawful duties.
Olekina, however, maintained that the matter raised fundamental questions about the distinction between institutional and personal liability, questioning why property belonging to a company with several shareholders could be targeted over an employment claim involving his Senate office.
He also accused Paran TV, which he claimed was linked to Kajiado Governor Joseph Ole Lenku, of amplifying what he described as misleading accounts of the incident for political purposes.
The senator said he would challenge what he termed the misuse of judicial processes and warned against using court orders as a justification for invading private property.
“I will not sit back and allow court processes or cheap propaganda to be weaponized as a licence to invade private property, defame my name, and intimidate citizens,” he said.
He added: “Let me be equally clear: anyone who trespasses onto private property should be ready to face the consequences. The rule of law must operate within its proper constitutional limits; anything less erodes justice and public trust in our institutions.”

Irrespective of res
items.text:
'He will see what Man Utd are made of' - Pulis on Pochettino's first game
- Published
Stepping into a job like Mauricio Pochettino has done at Manchester United, where managers have come and gone frequently, will always lead you to wonder why the others have not lasted very long.
Irrespective of results, you face these first few days in your new post with suspicion.
So, while what happens in Pochettino's first game against Liverpool on Sunday is important, it will not define his early opinions of the club - good or bad.
Whenever you take over a team in mid-season, which I did on a few occasions, you don't usually get much time to work with your players before your first game.
Jumping straight in and going straight to the heart of a two-day preparation for a game, like Pochettino has done before United go to Anfield, is so difficult and I am not sure any manager can honestly make a profound difference.
A change of voice helps, I'm sure, but so does showing strength and confidence in your own principles and making sure the players understand you demand complete and utter commitment in all the games you face, starting with this one.
With time on the training ground being so limited, my initial work would focus on us being a team and working up and down the pitch together, by breaking down different scenarios inside the game and what we should do in them.
I'd keep the focus on hard work and making us difficult to beat - clean sheets are so under-rated.
Then, on the day, your first pre-match speech is always a massive one, and it will be the same for Pochettino too.
My first team talk would always focus on generating an 'us against the world' mentality. As a manager coming in now, you've usually got the job because the team has struggled, so you can play on that to motivate the players.
You can use media reports and stories to show the negativity against them - but then counter that by producing a real 'stand-up and be counted' kind of rallying call, before sending them out on the pitch, while mentioning your faith in them to succeed.
'What your own eyes tell you is most important'
I would have selected my team before I met the players, through my own knowledge and also with help from within.
Whichever club I went in at, I'd expect to know something about most of the players within the group in terms of their position and ability, but understanding the character of the squad was vital too.
The existing staff would know more about the lads' qualities in that respect than myself or anyone who had just arrived with me, so I'd always discuss that with the people I had inherited, from fitness coaches to the medical department.
It's what your own eyes tell you that is most important, however. Going into your first game gives you the opportunity to see for yourself what your players are made of - and it can be a completely different view from what other people see.
Most of the early games I managed would be hit and miss in terms of selection, but I would quickly work out the strengths and weaknesses of the group.
As I've mentioned in previous columns, one of my first aims at any club where I was manager was about putting out a team, not a group of individuals.
It does not take long to see when that is not happening. I can remember my first game of my first spell at Stoke, a 4-2 defeat at Walsall in the Championship.
I wasn't universally enamoured by certain crowd favourites in that team and, while any manager knows that leaving some of them out could have an adverse effect on the supporters' view of yourself, you have to stand up and make decisions based on what you see.
It is the same if there are other issues with the squad you have inherited too.
West Brom's first game after I was appointed manager was a draw with West Ham on New Year's Day 2015.
I sat in the stands at Upton Park with my son, Anthony, who was concerned how different the Albion team was compared to Crystal Palace, the last team I had managed in the Premier League.
He was right to worry about it, but we still found a way - a totally different way of playing, but still a way to win that suited the group.
All your staff have to understand your objectives
My initial aims after arriving at any club mid-season were pretty direct and also pretty basic too.
The staff I inherited did not just know the players, they were also the first group who had to understand my objectives and also my principles - like the work ethic I expected, for example.
Irrespective of what they were used to doing, it was imperative they followed my lead.
One of the clubs I arrived at were struggling at the foot of the table and also suffering from a glut of injuries.
In my opinion, the players were taking advantage of a very honest and hard-working medical department, who were quite accommodating on the treatment times for the lads.
I changed that immediately, so injured players were treated at 9am, 2pm and 4pm, with sessions in-between those times for strength and recovery workouts.
This did not go down well with the players because it impeded on their social lives and, in one case, a player whose injury record was not exactly brilliant came to me complaining that his wife expected him to pick his children up from school and being asked to be in at 4pm affected his private life too.
I did not budge, and funnily enough the player in question recovered quite quickly - as did the majority of the other injured players.
'Clear the treatment rooms, and make sure the players are fit'
Asking injured players to be at the training ground all day was by far the best way of getting them fit, in my experience, and the medical departments I managed were all working well past 4pm anyway so it was no hardship to them.

items.title: Live: Finland says war 'spilling over' after Baltic Sea drone strike on Russian cargo ship
items.summary:
Finland warned the war in Ukraine was "spilling over" after a drone set ablaze a Russian cargo ship on the eastern Baltic Sea on Saturday. Helsinki stressed that Kyiv had the right to defend itself against Moscow's aggression. Follow our liveblog for the latest developments.
Two injured after apartm
items.text:
Finland warned the war in Ukraine was "spilling over" after a drone set ablaze a Russian cargo ship on the eastern Baltic Sea on Saturday. Helsinki stressed that Kyiv had the right to defend itself against Moscow's aggression. Follow our liveblog for the latest developments.
Two injured after apartment 'destroyed' in Kyiv Oblast, authorities say
Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv Oblast Military Administration, said that a five-story residential building was "destroyed" in the Vyshhorod district of Kyiv Oblast (📍), just north of the capital, after an overnight Russian drone strike. Two people were injured in the attack.
Tkachenko reported on Telegram that State Emergency Service units, psychologists and an emergency medical team were working at the scene.
In Ukraine, the fight to keep winter outside begins with a broken window
As winter sets in, Ukraine is facing a severe shortage of replacement windows with Russian missile and drone attacks continuing to damage buildings, leaving residents exposed to the cold. Temperatures in Kyiv fell to minus 20 degrees Celsius (minus 4 degrees Fahrenheit) last winter.
Government assistance can take months, skilled installers are in short supply and replacement costs have soared, hitting low-income districts near industrial zones hardest.
To address the shortage, the industry is investing in training. A vocational college in Kyiv opened a European Union-funded facility in March, where 26 10th graders have started a three-year program to become window, door and facade installers.
The program was established after professional associations lobbied the government to formally recognize window installation as a profession, allowing the industry to access grants and create structured training courses.
Graduates can expect starting salaries of around $900, on par with law graduates due to Ukraine’s acute skill drain, according to Mykhailo Orlenko, executive director of the Association of Ukrainian Manufacturers of Transparent Structure.
Ukraine war is 'spilling over', Finland says
A Ukrainian drone hit a Russian cargo ship which caught fire on the eastern Baltic Sea, as Finland's prime minister said Kyiv had the right to hit back against its "aggressor".
Hours later, a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating Finnish airspace, according to the Finnish defence minister, who drew a possible link between the two incidents.
Finland's Prime Minister Petteri Orpo suggested it had to do with the Ukraine-Russia war started by Moscow's 2022 invasion.
"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity... Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor," Orpo said on X.
UK, Netherlands PMs meet and commit to keep supporting Ukraine, Downing Street says
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham met Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten and committed to giving Ukraine the support it needs to resist Russia's invasion and "secure a lasting, durable peace", a Downing Street spokesperson said in a statement published late Saturday.
"Both leaders agreed on the vital need to keep the pressure up on Russia to bring (Russian President Vladimir) Putin to the negotiations table," the statement said.

items.text:
Dozens missing as deadly fire hits Indonesian candy factory
November 22, 2026
Indonesian rescue teams are searching for 36 workers who remained unaccounted for after a fire at a candy-making factory killed at least three people, officials said on Sunday.
The fire occurred at the Fonusa Agung Mulia factory, around 50 kilometers (31 miles) west of the capital, Jakarta, in the Serang district of Banten province.
What do we know about the Indonesian confectionery factory fire?
The factory caught fire on Saturday afternoon, local search and rescue agency official Rizky Dwianto said.
"All elements of the joint SAR (search-and-rescue) team are making maximum effort to locate the victims while prioritizing the safety of personnel in the field," he added.
Rizky said four people injured in the blaze had been taken to a nearby hospital and health clinic. Eleven more were said to have been rescued alive.
The governor of Banten province, Andra Soni, told reporters overnight that 60 people were believed to have been inside the factory when the fire broke out.
Drone footage shows the fire destroyed large sections of the three-story building, bringing down the roof in some places.
Survivors said the fire started in a cooling unit on the third floor.
The factory produces Milkita, an Indonesian brand of milk-based candies and snack products.
Deadly industrial fires in Indonesia
Indonesia has seen a series of deadly industrial fires in recent years, raising questions about the country's workplace safety standards into question.
Among other disasters, at least 22 people were killed in a fire last December that broke out in a seven-story building in Jakarta after a suspected drone battery explosion, police said.
An explosion in a nickel-processing plant in the east of the country killed at least 13 people in 2023.

items.text:
Dozens missing after fire at Indonesian factory
- Published
At least three people have been killed and 36 were still missing after a fire at a confectionary factory in western Java on Saturday.
Firefighters were still tackling some flames on Sunday, while rescuers searched for the missing in parts of the damaged building where workers were believed to be trapped.
Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency said on Sunday 15 survivors had been located, and four others taken to hospital and a local clinic with undisclosed injuries.
The factory is in Serang district, Banten province, about 50km west of Jakarta. Authorities have not yet determined the fire's cause.
Banten Governor, Andra Soni, told media about 60 people were believed to be inside the factory when it caught fire.
Photos and footage of the scene showed the large factory taken over by flames during the night, firefighters battling the flames, and first responders retrieving at least one body from the wreckage on Sunday morning.
"All members of the joint SAR team are making every effort to locate the missing victims while prioritising the safety of personnel on the ground," the rescue agency said.
Relatives of the missing workers had gathered outside the factory waiting for updates, according to local broadcasts cited by AFP.
Firefighters had been called to the building at 1630 local time (0930 GMT) but it was already engulfed in flames, broadcaster Kompas TV reported, citing fire official Tubugas Machfudz.
"When we arrived (on location)... a large area was already on fire. So we could not determine whether the company's protection system was functioning properly or not," he said.
The factory is owned by PT Fonusa Agung Mulia, according to search and rescue authorities.
On LinkedIn the company describes itself as a subsidiary of UNIFAM, one of Indonesia's largest food and beverage companies.

items.title: Sifuna accuses Ruto administration of failing Kenyans in Diaspora, pledges better consular services
items.summary: NAIROBI,Kenya Nov 22 – Linda Mwananchi party leader Edwin Sifuna has accused President William Ruto’s administration of neglecting Kenyans living abroad, pledging sweeping improvements in consular services and stronger government support for citizens in the diaspora if his political camp assumes pow
items.text:
NAIROBI,Kenya Nov 22 – Linda Mwananchi party leader Edwin Sifuna has accused President William Ruto’s administration of neglecting Kenyans living abroad, pledging sweeping improvements in consular services and stronger government support for citizens in the diaspora if his political camp assumes power.
Sifuna said the current administration had failed to match the financial contribution of Kenyans abroad with efficient public services, leaving many struggling to access basic documentation and government assistance despite billions of shillings remitted home.
He singled out the Kenyan Embassy in Washington, saying understaffing and bureaucratic inefficiencies had subjected citizens to prolonged delays in accessing essential consular services, including national identity cards.
Speaking during the opening of Linda Mwananchi’s first international office in New Jersey, Sifuna said his previous engagements with Kenyans across the United States had exposed deep-seated dissatisfaction with the government’s handling of diaspora affairs.
He said Kenyans living abroad had increasingly felt abandoned by a government that readily benefits from their remittances but fails to provide adequate support when they need assistance.
“Kenyans living abroad do not feel that their government is there for them as much as they are there for their country. The resources you remit through hard labour are not commensurate with the level of services you receive,” he said.
Sifuna recalled visiting Texas, Houston, Maryland and Washington during a 2024 trip to the US, where he said he encountered widespread complaints over the inadequacy of consular services and the government’s apparent indifference to diaspora concerns.
He cited the limited staffing at the Washington embassy, claiming that the facility had only one legal counsellor, a situation he said contributed to delays in delivering basic services.
The Nairobi Senator argued that Kenya’s diplomatic missions should be measured by their ability to serve citizens rather than the number of embassies established abroad.
He called for a deliberate redistribution of consular resources to areas with substantial Kenyan populations, saying the government should prioritise accessibility and efficiency over the symbolic expansion of diplomatic missions.
“Rather than opening embassies in Europe just to feel good, consular support services should be deployed efficiently where large concentrations of Kenyans actually reside,” he said.
Sifuna also accused the Ruto administration of failing in its responsibility to protect Kenyans caught up in international conflicts, citing citizens who allegedly ended up fighting for Russia in its war against Ukraine.
As a member of the Senate Defence Committee, he said he had raised the plight of missing Kenyans and those reportedly held as prisoners of war in Ukraine, but criticised Foreign Affairs Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi for failing to provide definitive answers to distressed families.
He claimed Mudavadi had sought to defer the matter until January when he appeared before the committee, prolonging the uncertainty surrounding the fate of the affected Kenyans.
Sifuna said expectations had been high that President Ruto’s visit to Russia would yield a diplomatic breakthrough, particularly a deal to secure the release and repatriation of Kenyans caught up in the conflict.
However, he expressed disappointment that the visit did not produce the anticipated announcement, arguing that the protection and welfare of Kenyan citizens abroad should rank among the government’s foremost responsibilities.
He contrasted Kenya’s response with that of other countries which deploy aircraft and naval vessels to evacuate their nationals from conflict zones, saying Nairobi must demonstrate similar commitment to the safety of its citizens.
The Linda Mwananchi leader said his political movement intended to pursue a more responsive diaspora policy, with the New Jersey office marking the beginning of efforts to establish a structured presence among Kenyans living abroad.
He urged Kenyans across the US, including those in Houston, Washington DC and Seattle, to rally behind the movement, saying diaspora communities would have a greater role in shaping its political agenda.
Sifuna said the movement had retained key leadership positions, including secretaries for diaspora affairs and international affairs, to strengthen engagement and coordination with supporters outside Kenya.
He also pledged to introduce transparent mechanisms for diaspora participation, particularly in political fundraising and mobilisation, following complaints by some supporters who had contributed personal resources to previous campaigns but felt sidelined afterwards.
He said the movement would establish formal structures to ensure supporters understood how resources were being utilised and had clear channels through which to participate in political activities.
Sifuna maintained that Kenyans in the diaspora were equal stakeholders in the country’s future, insisting that their financial contribution, political opinions and electoral choices deserved recognition.
“The entire purpose of this visit is to listen to you. Your views matter, your contribution to the development of our country matters, and your vote matters,” he said.

items.text:
COP31: Fossil fuels still missing from draft deal at UN climate summit
Published November 20, 2026last updated November 22, 2026
What you need to know
- Diplomats and delegates from nearly 200 countries are meeting in Antalya, Turkey
- Like in previous years, the climate summit has been extended until a consensus is reached
- The latest COP31 draft deal still fails to mention fossil fuels, raising the possibility the summit could end with no deal
- Fossil fuels are a major flashpoint at this year's summit, which comes amid soaring energy prices and tensions over the US-Israeli war with Iran
These are the major developments from the closing phase of the UN's COP31 Climate Summit in Antalya, Turkey, on Friday, November 20 through Sunday, November 22:
What we know about the latest COP31 draft deal
The third draft makes no mention of the words "fossil," "oil," "coal," or "phase out."
However, as in the second draft, the latest version retains a goal to boost electricity's share of global energy use to 35% by 2035, as well as efforts to expand the use of "clean energy."
The draft text also does not stipulate that the "35-by-35" electrification target should be met using renewable energy sources.
It also urges countries to "accelerate" carbon capture and storage — a controversial technology backed by the fossil fuel industry.
Fossil fuels still missing in latest COP31 draft deal
Welcome back to our coverage of the UN's COP31 climate summit in Turkey.
The latest, and potentially final, version of the deal still makes no explicit mention of fossil fuels.
It does refer to a 2023 agreement that committed the world to transitioning away from fossil fuels — but stops short of naming them directly.
The third and presumably final draft text to emerge from negotiations at COP31, which lacks any mention of fossil fuels or how to transition away from them, has been rejected by NGOs.
In a statement, Teresa Anderson, Climate Justice Lead at ActionAid International, said the people who will benefit most from the new "35-by-35" electrification targets and carbon capture "are the fossil fuel, nuclear, data and CCUS (carbon capture, use and storage) industries.
"This text will help elites to profit while leaving people in the dark," Anderson said.
Brandon Wu, AAUSA's Director of Policy and Campaigns, said: "Rich countries came to the COP31 talks with nothing to offer other than red lines.
"They put forward meaningless fossil fuel transition roadmaps that were nothing more than restatements of inadequate existing policy, then hypocritically blamed developing countries for failing to take action on phasing out fossil fuels.
“This is the behaviour of an arrogant bully who cares about nothing but himself and it is no way to have a proper negotiation. COP31 was one of the worst COPs ever, and it’s because the EU and other developed countries came with zero spirit of solidarity, cooperation or compromise."
We're pausing our coverage
As COP31 extends into a second day of overtime, we are pausing our coverage.
In the early hours of Sunday, COP31 President and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum informed delegates at a plenary that a third and "final" text would be sent to them for review.
He added that negotiators would have until 6:00 am (0400 GMT) "to come to us with agreement on the text" and that a closing plenary would then be convened at 9:00 am local time.
Stay tuned for more news in the coming hours.
IN DEPTH: Why electrification is the climate game changer we need
The shift to green tech is already in full swing, including electric cars, electric buses, solar panels and heat pumps. But what is so electrifying about the latest wave of electrification?
Climate activist blames rich countries for COP failure
Harjeet Singh, the global convener of the Fill the Fund campaign and strategic advisor to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, said that COP31 could be a failure due to a lack of funding.
"COP31 is stuck for one simple reason: money. Europe and other rich countries came to Antalya with empty pockets," he wrote in a statement shared with multiple reporters.
"They've spent two weeks pushing electrification targets and demanding more ambition from developing countries, while refusing to pay for any of it," he added.
Singh accused wealthy countries of blocking a just transition mechanism and of ignoring calls to increase funding for the Adaptation Fund and the Loss and Damage Fund.
"You can't ask developing countries to transform their economies while they're drowning in disasters and debt," he wrote.
The climate activist stressed that the reason this COP failed wasn't a lack of solutions. It was due to "a lack of money and a lack of will from those who caused this crisis," he said.
IN DEPTH: Why is carbon capture not moving faster?
Carbon capture technology works, but its real-world capabilities are nowhere near to moving the needle on climate change. So what's the hold-up?
IN DEPTH: At COP31, conflict over climate science slows action on global warming
Attacks on climate science and disinformation seem to be delaying key decisions as the UN climate talks draw to a close in Antalya.
IN DEPTH: Africa at COP31 — Will climate cash finally flow?
Leaders from Africa, one of the continents worst hit by climate change, have spent years lobbying for hundreds of billions of dollars to help adapt to the rising impacts of global warming.
The rest of the world relies on African nations for their abundant natural resources, many of them used in clean energy production.
Yet at COP31, wealthy nations have so far failed to commit to the financing needed to help developing nations make a just transition.
Read our report from DW's Kathy Wood.
Peru blames 'geopolitical divisions' for lack of COP31 progress

items.title: Ruto makes unannounced trip to Congo, abruptly ends Western tour
items.summary: NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 22 – President William Ruto has cut short his Western Kenya development tour to attend a high-level diplomatic meeting in the Republic of Congo, where he is expected to hold talks with three other African leaders amid strained relations between Kenya and the Democratic Republic of
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 22 – President William Ruto has cut short his Western Kenya development tour to attend a high-level diplomatic meeting in the Republic of Congo, where he is expected to hold talks with three other African leaders amid strained relations between Kenya and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).
Ruto arrived in Oyo on Saturday, November 21, 2026, ahead of Sunday’s four-nation meeting convened by Republic of Congo President Denis Sassou-N’Guesso.
The President’s departure came just days after he launched an extensive development tour of Western Kenya, which began on Thursday, November 19, and was scheduled to run in two phases, concluding on December 1.
According to the programme outlined by Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi, the first phase was due to run from November 19 to 24, before resuming on November 28 and ending on December 1.
Ruto’s abrupt departure therefore interrupted the first leg of the tour, which was expected to take him through Busia, Bungoma, Kakamega and Vihiga counties.
In a departure from his usual foreign travel arrangements, the President’s trip to Congo was not publicly announced by State House before his departure. His arrival was confirmed by the Congolese presidency in a statement posted on its official X account on Saturday.
“His Excellency Mr William Ruto, President of the Republic of Kenya, arrived in Oyo on Saturday, November 21, to take part in a high-level four-party meeting initiated by the Congolese President, His Excellency Mr Denis Sassou-N’Guesso,” the statement said.
The meeting will bring together Ruto, Sassou-N’Guesso, DRC President Félix Tshisekedi and Togo’s President of the Council, Faure Gnassingbé.
The diplomatic engagement comes against the backdrop of strained relations between Nairobi and Kinshasa, with the four leaders expected to discuss regional relations and tensions in the Great Lakes region.
The disagreement between Kenya and the DRC escalated in December 2023 following the launch of the Alliance Fleuve Congo (AFC), a political-military coalition associated with the M23 rebel movement, in Nairobi.
Kinshasa protested the event, accusing Kenya of providing a platform to a group it considers hostile. Nairobi, however, maintained that it could not restrict political expression.
Relations were further strained in October 2025 when Nairobi hosted a political gathering involving Congolese opposition figures, including former DRC President Joseph Kabila.
Gnassingbé’s participation adds a wider regional dimension to the meeting, given his involvement in African Union-led mediation efforts aimed at addressing tensions in the Great Lakes region.
Although the Congolese presidency confirmed the four-party meeting, it had not released a detailed agenda by Saturday.
Ruto’s trip comes at a politically sensitive moment, with his administration also seeking to consolidate support in Western Kenya ahead of the 2027 General Election. The President had been using the regional tour to launch development projects and rally residents behind his administration’s agenda.

Las Vegas GP: Max Verstappen wins wild race as Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc collide again
Max Verstappen wins wild Las Vegas Grand Prix; Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri claim double podium for McLaren after late Mercedes collapse saw George Russell and Kimi Antonelli drop back; Charles Leclerc penalised for causing collision with Ferrari team-mate Lewis Hamilton
Sunday 22 November 2026 05:56, UK
Max Verstappen produced a remarkable drive to win a wild Las Vegas Grand Prix that saw him withstand extreme pressure from George Russell and Kimi Antonelli before a late Mercedes collapse.
Pole-sitter Verstappen retained the lead at the start but the enormous power of a slipstream on the long straights of the Las Vegas Strip Circuit made it impossible for the leader to pull clear.
First Russell, and then later newly crowned world champion Antonelli were each able to pass Verstappen on several occasions but the Red Bull driver calmly retook the lead within a few corners every time, expertly managing the deployment of his power.

Russell, trying to pass his team-mate for second with three laps remaining, ran into a barrier after overshooting a corner and dropped down the order, before Antonelli appeared to suffer a deployment issue at the start of the final lap that allowed Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri to snatch a double podium for McLaren.
There was more unwanted drama for Ferrari as team-mates Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc collided again as they battled for sixth with 12 laps remaining, with the latter given a 10-second penalty by the stewards for causing the incident.
Pierre Gasly took fifth ahead of his team-mate Franco Colapinto to secure a major points haul for Alpine, with Hamilton recovering to seventh, having served a 10-second penalty himself earlier in the race for overtaking Norris off track.
Carlos Sainz snatched eighth from Russell on the run to the finish line to equal Williams' best result of the season, while Leclerc claimed the final point in 10th.

items.title: Kenyans in Diaspora offer Sifuna billions to build JKIA if he wins the presidency
items.summary: NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 22 – Kenyans living in the United States have challenged Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna to tap into the financial muscle of the diaspora to fund the expansion of Jomo Kenyatta International Airport (JKIA), saying they are capable of mobilising resources for the project without invo
items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 22 – Kenyans living in the United States have challenged Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna to tap into the financial muscle of the diaspora to fund the expansion of Jomo Kenyatta International Airport (JKIA), saying they are capable of mobilising resources for the project without involving foreign investors.
The diaspora community said Kenyans abroad could pool their financial contributions and partner with the government to modernise the country’s main airport, cautioning Sifuna against pursuing another arrangement similar to the controversial deal with India’s Adani Group.
The proposal was presented by Kiemo Mohando, a Kenyan based in Columbus, Ohio, during a meeting with Sifuna and other Linda Mwananchi supporters in New Jersey on Saturday.
Mohando said Kenyans abroad had demonstrated their financial capacity through billions of shillings sent home annually and could channel part of the resources towards financing major infrastructure projects.
He challenged the community to move beyond individual remittances and establish a coordinated funding arrangement that would allow them to participate directly in the country’s development.
“We can build the airport. Don’t look for another Adani. We can build an airport. We can reorganise ourselves, let’s partner with the government, let’s do the airport,” Mohando said.
He maintained that the diaspora’s collective financial strength could provide an alternative to expensive infrastructure financing arrangements, which often attract public scrutiny over their terms and long-term implications.
“You see how much money we sent to Kenya. Yes. It’s a lot of it’s billions, right? We can build the airport,” he said.
Mohando also called for mechanisms that would allow diaspora members to contribute directly to development institutions, arguing that such an arrangement would strengthen transparency and accountability in the use of funds.
His proposal comes against the backdrop of the contentious JKIA expansion plan that brought the government under pressure in 2024 after it sought to enter into a long-term concession arrangement with Adani Airport Holdings.
The Adani controversy
The proposed deal, estimated at $1.85 billion, was designed to facilitate the construction of a second runway and a new passenger terminal at JKIA, alongside improvements to existing airport infrastructure.
Under the proposal, Adani Airport Holdings would have financed the project in exchange for a 30-year concession to operate the airport, raising concerns over the potential transfer of control of a strategic national asset to a private company.
The arrangement sparked resistance from aviation workers, who feared job losses and changes to their employment terms, as well as questions over the procurement process, transparency and the financial obligations Kenya would assume.
The Law Society of Kenya and the Kenya Human Rights Commission challenged the proposal in court, arguing that the arrangement raised constitutional and public procurement concerns.
The controversy intensified in November 2024 when Gautam Adani, the conglomerate’s founder, and other executives were indicted in the United States over allegations of bribery and securities fraud linked to energy contracts in India. The allegations were denied and did not constitute a conviction.
On November 21, 2024, President William Ruto announced the cancellation of the proposed JKIA procurement process, citing new information from investigative agencies and international partners.
The decision also affected a separate proposed electricity transmission partnership involving Adani, effectively bringing the group’s major infrastructure ambitions in Kenya to an abrupt halt.
The collapse of the airport proposal left the government under pressure to identify alternative financing arrangements for JKIA’s expansion as demand for air travel and airport capacity continued to grow.
The diaspora proposal now introduces another option into the debate, with Mohando arguing that Kenyans abroad should be considered development partners rather than merely sources of remittances.
Sifuna courts diaspora backing
The meeting was part of Sifuna’s engagements with Kenyans in the United States, where he officially opened the first international office of the Linda Mwananchi Movement in New Jersey.
The Nairobi Senator used the occasion to criticise the government over what he described as persistent neglect of Kenyans living abroad, particularly in the delivery of consular services and protection of citizens caught up in international conflicts.
He argued that despite their substantial contribution to the economy, Kenyans in the diaspora continued to face bureaucratic hurdles when seeking government assistance.
Sifuna also called for stronger diaspora structures within the movement, saying Kenyans abroad should have a transparent platform through which they could contribute to political activities and participate in shaping the country’s future.
He said the visit was intended to listen to their concerns and establish lasting channels of engagement.
“The entire purpose of this visit is to listen to you. Your views matter, your contribution to the development of our country matters, and your vote matters,” Sifuna said.

items.text:
New draft deal aims to avert collapse of talks at climate summit
- Published
Talks were set to resume at the UN COP31 summit on Sunday for a second day of overtime as countries struggled to reach a new global climate deal.
A new draft agreement was published in the early hours of Sunday which the Turkey and Australia co-hosts hoped would bridge the divide between nations.
Although it still includes no specific reference to "transitioning away from fossil fuels" - an omission in the previous draft that sparked threats of walkouts - it does acknowledge a previous commitment made by countries to do just that three years ago.
And it includes for the first time a recognition that the world is on track to miss the crucial goal of keeping temperatures below 1.5C of warming.
The EU and Pacific states had been arguing against the removal of fossil fuels from the draft text. The EU has not yet reacted to this latest draft.
The Africa Group is likely to be disappointed at this latest iteration as it includes no specific figure on money for adaptation and instead kicks that decision to future meetings.
Countries were expected to reconvene at 09:00 local time (06:00GMT) to decide whether to approve a new deal.
If countries cannot reach consensus - as required by the UN's climate talks process - the negotiations could be suspended until next year. This has only happened once before since countries started holding COP climate meetings in 1995.
Just hours before the new text was published, EU Commissioner for Climate Wopke Hoekstra said if the bloc could not get "what is needed in terms of climate action... then there's no deal."
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, the UK's chief negotiator, struck a more hopeful tone, saying her team was still working to get an agreement.
A draft deal unveiled earlier this week called for a faster phase-out of fossil fuels, but a second, pared-down version released on Thursday stripped away all mentions of coal, oil and gas - sparking threats of a walk out.
The fallout led to the summit in Antalya blowing past the original deadline of Friday. On Saturday negotiating teams who had Sunday morning flights were rescheduling them - a sign a deal was still not in sight, and raising the risk that as teams eventually had to leave, the meeting could lose the critical numbers needed to pass an agreement.
As part of a last ditch effort to produce an acceptable text, the European Union and Saudi Arabia - who were deeply divided over the future of fossil fuels - were brought together on Saturday to seek a compromise.
COP31 President and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum told delegates in the early hours of Sunday he believed concerns had been addressed.
"We ask you to look at this decision carefully," Kurum said. "We are closer than ever to agreement on the remaining issues."
What has the issue been?
Ministers from Panama, Solomon Islands, Cote d'Ivoire and the EU were fighting to have a commitment to move away from fossil fuels put back into the final agreement, after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi Arabia pushed for its removal.
"It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.
Tuvalu's Climate Minister Maina Talia told reporters it was a "red line" for the low-lying Pacific nation: "We're talking about the root cause of all of this".
France's Minister of Ecological Transition, Monique Barbut, took aim at several references in the text to carbon capture, use and storage (CCUS) - the technology that takes emissions when they are released and stores them underground - as a licence for other countries to keep burning oil and gas.
"We cannot be announcing to the world that we are now getting to 1.5 increase in the temperature and do business like nothing was happening," Barbut said.
In the latest text the commitments to CCUS have been reduced, which may be enough to alleviate the EU's concerns.
For the first time at a COP, the agreement - known officially as the Antalya Accords - could acknowledge that the goal set under the Paris climate accord of keeping global temperature rise below 1.5C has been missed.
The world is entering a period called "overshoot".
Beyond this point scientists warn millions more people will be exposed to sea level rise and extreme heat.
But Australia's Climate Change and Energy Minister, Chris Bowen, who is leading negotiations, pushed back on the need to include language on fossil fuels.
He argued the summit was about implementation, and should focus on the move towards clean energy sources.
'We did not come here to beg'
One of the other key issues raised by developing nations - the lack of money - appears unresolved in the latest draft agreement.
Earlier versions of the text included an agreement to ramp up money for adaptation to $120bn (£91bn) by 2035 - a figure that was then removed.
"We did not come here to beg, we came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries," said Zanetor Agyeman Rawlings, Ghana's Environment Minister and chair of the African Group of negotiators.
Climate activists and environmental groups, who are observers to these talks, have slammed negotiations.
"I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst COP ever," said Mohamed Adow of Powershift Africa.

items.text:
Displaced Darfur families face volatile winter as Sudan aid cuts bite
Sudan’s displacement crisis could worsen with winter approaching.
Omdurman, Sudan – When Fatima Mohamed Haroun was displaced from West Darfur state at the start of Sudan’s war in 2023, she never imagined she would find herself caring for four of her grandchildren far from her home.
Haroun, who believes she is aged about 60, said her son went missing a year ago. His wife died after giving birth, leaving Haroun as the sole guardian of her four grandchildren.
Now living in a crumbling mudbrick building in al-Ghadir, north of Omdurman, in Khartoum state, she has received no humanitarian assistance since her displacement.
Without an income, it is only the goodwill of her neighbours that prevents Haroun and her grandchildren from starving. But every day is a battle to find food, water or medicine, and with winter fast approaching, proper shelter, warm clothes, and blankets for the children are another priority.
“I cannot work or earn money, so we depend on neighbours who occasionally give us food. But even our neighbours sometimes have nothing to eat. When they have no food, my grandchildren and I go to bed hungry,” she told Al Jazeera.
“We have no supplies to help us cope with the cold, not even blankets to keep us warm. We sleep on the ground with only the sky above us. The cold is severe, and the children are suffering. We appeal to the government and humanitarian organisations to provide food, blankets, covers and other basic necessities to help us endure the cold and protect our children.”
Temperatures can drop significantly in Omdurman during the winter, and at night al-Ghadir can be particularly cold due to its location close to mountainous areas. Displaced families living in temporary shelters here are especially vulnerable because they lack blankets, winter clothing and heating facilities.
The war in Sudan, which broke out between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary in April 2023, has led to one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.
Khartoum state, which was initially one of the epicentres of the war but is now relatively more stable, continues to host large numbers of people forced to flee their homes, particularly from southern and western Sudan where fighting is ongoing. Millions of people in areas such as Darfur have experienced or are at risk of horrific violence, forcing them to flee to other parts of Sudan or neighbouring countries where they live in horrendous conditions.
As of July 30, Khartoum state was hosting 414,252 internally displaced people, according to data from the International Organization for Migration’s (IOM) Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM).
Winter is expected to worsen conditions for families living in temporary shelters or unfinished buildings without adequate blankets and warm clothing.
Sudan has more than 8.5 million internally displaced people, according to DTM Sudan, with the IOM and the United Nations refugee agency (UNHCR) warning that millions are still without a roof over their heads and risk losing access to emergency shelters due to funding shortages.
About 15.4 million people in Sudan need emergency shelter and basic household items. The agencies said funding shortages mean humanitarian organisations can prioritise assistance for only 10 percent of those in need, leaving millions without support.
Fighting, general insecurity, drone attacks on civilian infrastructure and camps, as well as other logistical challenges were all obstructing aid deliveries, the agencies said. Less than half of the funding for Sudan’s 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, which requires $2.9bn to assist 20.4 million people in need, had been received, forcing humanitarian agencies to scale back some services.
Abdelaziz Suleiman Ori, director of culture and information for the Darfur regional government, said his administration was monitoring the conditions for displaced people in host states, including Khartoum, and coordinating humanitarian assistance.
The regional government has drawn up a winter plan that includes blankets, clothing and food to respond to the impending crisis, but Ori acknowledged that available resources were so far insufficient.
“Since the outbreak of the war on April 15, Governor Minni Arko Minawi has dispatched humanitarian convoys from Port Sudan to el-Fasher, passing through Madani, Kosti and El Obeid. We are also in contact with international organisations and UN agencies to monitor the situation of displaced people in different states,” Ori told Al Jazeera.
“Our winter plan includes blankets, clothing, food and children’s necessities. But our resources are not enough to meet the needs of the large number of displaced people. We appeal to humanitarian partners to provide more support.”
Ori said that only a collective response – involving regional government, host states, local authorities and NGOs – can properly respond to the crisis.
“Responsibility for displaced people is shared between the regional government, host states, local communities and humanitarian organisations,” he said.
“We coordinate efforts, seek relief assistance and monitor their conditions with local authorities. We bear part of the responsibility, but need greater cooperation to ease their suffering.”
Kheira Matar Hassan, a resident of Darfur, passed through Renk, Rabak and Khartoum at the start of the war before settling in al-Ghadir camp in 2023. She became separated from her husband when he went looking for work in a gold mining area in Chad at the same time.
She has received no word from him since he disappeared and has been left alone to support their seven children. They live in a dilapidated home built of bricks and mud bricks with damaged areas covered with cloth and plastic sheeting.
