items.text:
Bahrain says Iranian attack causes fire at industrial facility
Bahrain reports no injuries, as Iran’s IRGC says it targeted US military positions at two bases in al-Riffa and Awali.
Bahrain says an Iranian attack has struck a civilian industrial facility, starting a fire, in the latest escalation of the war in the Middle East.
Bahrain’s Defence Force said its air defences intercepted a number of Iranian aerial attacks late on Saturday.
In a post on X, Bahrain’s Ministry of Interior said the attack was part of “Iranian aggression”.
It said preliminary reports pointed to material damage but no injuries, and that civil defence teams were working to bring the fire under control.
The Interior Ministry did not name the facility or say where it was. Earlier, air raid sirens sounded in Bahrain, and the ministry urged residents to move to the nearest safe place without saying what the threat was.
In a statement after the attack, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it had carried out a combined missile and drone operation targeting United States military positions at the al-Riffa and Awali bases in Bahrain.
The IRGC claimed it destroyed two US Patriot air defence radars at the bases.
The attack was “in response to continued aggression and violations of the airspace of the Islamic Republic of Iran”, the statement said.
“After two US MQ-1 and MQ-9 reconnaissance and combat drones violated Iranian airspace, US military positions at the aforementioned bases were targeted in an operation by the IRGC Aerospace Force,” it added.
Earlier, Iran’s semi-official Fars news agency reported that the IRGC had attacked two military bases used by US forces at Sheikh Isa and Juffair.
However, Iran’s state news agency IRNA reported that an interceptor missile launched from the US Fifth Fleet base in Bahrain had crashed on Sitra Island and started a large fire. It cited an outlet called Bahrain News, which blamed a recurring malfunction in the Patriot air defence system.
Bahrain hosts the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet. It has been attacked repeatedly since the war began, including three drone attacks in recent days after a lull of several weeks.
Gulf Arab states have come under repeated fire from Tehran since the US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28.

items.text:
Raya set to have scan on injury - how much would Arsenal miss him?
- Published
Injuries are never good news, but Arsenal's latest one to first-choice goalkeeper David Raya has come in the worst possible position.
The 31-year-old was forced to leave the pitch 70 minutes into Saturday's 2-2 draw with Newcastle, appearing to hurt his shoulder in an innocuous challenge with Magpies forward William Osula.
The Gunners arguably have the best depth in the league with at least two quality options in all outfield positions after a period of squad strengthening.
In goal, however, cover appears much thinner.
Raya was a key component in Arsenal's Premier League title-winning campaign last season, was named in the Fifpro Men's World 11 and was unlucky to not win the Yashin Trophy, awarded to the world's best goalkeeper, which went to Spain team-mate Unai Simon.
Behind him, Kepa Arrizabalaga still holds the record as the most expensive goalkeeper in football history following his £72m move from Athletic Bilbao to Chelsea in August 2018, but is far behind Raya in terms of quality.
Raya's passing range and ability on the ball are key to how Arsenal build their attacks, and his presence is a big reason why they have the best defence in the league.
They have conceded just seven Premier League goals this season, with only Brighton able to match that tally - having played a game fewer.
Arsenal also brought in former Leeds goalkeeper Illan Meslier on a free transfer in the summer but his only appearance this season came in the embarrassing Carabao Cup defeat by League Two Fleetwood.
When asked about Raya's injury, Arteta said he did not know how severe the issue is.
"Well, unfortunately, he had to come off, which is never good news," said Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta.
"He will get assessed now, and probably he will have an MRI [scan] tomorrow to see what it is exactly he has done.
"I don't know how it happened, and what the injury is at the moment, so we'll have to wait and see tomorrow."
- Who was 'a consistent threat'? Newcastle v Arsenal player ratings 
  - Published2 hours ago
'Raya the one player Arsenal can't afford to lose'
Arsenal are about to enter a gruelling period of games - with or without Raya.
In the next four weeks, they face Borussia Dortmund, Manchester City, Brentford, Tottenham Hotspur and Real Madrid.
"The one player that Arsenal cannot afford to lose is David Raya," said former England forward Alan Shearer, who is a pundit on Saturday's BBC Match of the Day. "He has made such a difference since joining from Brentford in 2023.
"They have top-class cover in just about every other position but he is the one individual that Mikel Arteta will be thinking 'we don't want to play without him for an extended period'. They could, of course go into the transfer market if they need to in January, but Arteta will be desperately hoping Raya is not out for long."
Raya is reportedly close to agreeing a new deal at the club, which shows his importance to the Gunners with two years remaining on his contract.
Ex-England midfielder Jamie Redknapp said on Sky Sports that Raya is "irreplaceable".
"Kepa is not up to the level of him - I actually think he struggles in the Premier League," added Redknapp. "Obviously we've seen in the Carabao Cup last year in the final.
"He is now going to have to play some games and that's going to be difficult for him.
"It will change everything for Arsenal for a while so that's a massive blow depending on how long David Raya is out because he is irreplaceable - probably the best goalkeeper in the Premier League, if not one of the best in the world."

items.text:
We got two very different pictures of Nvidia this week, depending on whether you were focused on the company’s latest earnings report or the tech executives loudly calling for former CEO Jensen Huang’s return.
On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Kirsten Korosec, Tim De Chant, and I discussed the latest news from the AI chipmaker, which reported soaring revenue and insisted that it has no plans for Huang to return.
Kirsten described this as “the tale of two Nvidias this week,” with the company’s current executives assuring investors, “Hey, we’ve got this.” At the same time, “You’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back, circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back.” (The company’s falling stock price certainly suggests that Wall Street isn’t feeling reassured.)
Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.
Kirsten Korosec: Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China. This was coming directly from the interim CEO Colette Kress, and that coincides with the Trump administration also talking about closing off what we have discussed in the past, which is this idea of remote access — really closing and tightening all these restrictions [so] the chips can’t make it into China.
What was happening is that data centers were being set up right outside, in countries like Malaysia and elsewhere, and then companies within China were remote accessing these chips, and so that’s now also been shut down.
A lot is happening on the China front that is so much bigger than Nvidia, but Nvidia came out publicly and said, “Nope, we’re shutting this part down.” I’ll be very curious to see if this changes, maybe in the first half of 2027.
Tim De Chant: I’d love to be a fly on the wall in some of these Trump administration conversations, because they were much more stringent in terms of export controls at the end of the first Trump administration, and that continued through the Biden administration, where they really restricted Nvidia’s ability to export chips to China. I think that something changed in the last couple of years that really opened Nvidia’s ability to sell in the country.
Anthony Ha: One of the things that really surprised me as we were preparing for this episode was [learning that critics] of Nvidia’s stance towards China estimate that 20% of their business comes from China.
And again, that’s not something you’re going to see directly in their financials, because that’s not direct sales to Chinese companies. But they’re saying, “A lot of the chips that are getting sold to companies in Malaysia or other companies in East Asia or Southeast Asia are going to end up [used by companies in] China eventually.” And so that could be — if Nvidia is really serious about this, I think this is something that’s very much in flux — that could actually be a pretty significant blow to their bottom line.
Kirsten: Although Nvidia’s bottom line is doing just fine. In every possible way, their guidance was incredible. They beat expectations. They have a long pipeline.
It was really interesting because you have that happening, and then you have all this noise happening in social media, and also a number of other tech conferences were happening this past week — Dealbook Summit, there [were] a few others in which you had the highest profile people that you can think of in the tech world commenting on Jensen [Huang], and Jensen himself commenting.
So it’s like the tale of two Nvidias this week. You’ve got the earnings and the current executives really talking about, “Hey, we’ve got this.” In fact, that was the last line that Collette Kress said [on the earnings call]. And then at the exact same time, or in parallel, you’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back, circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back. So it’s really quite the drama that we are definitely not done with, by the way.
Anthony: Although I think that what the folks who’d like to see Jensen Huang come back would say is that this most recent quarter is the last quarter under him. This is the [last of the] good times that we’re seeing under him. And so we don’t know how well Nvidia will do without him.
It seems like Nvidia’s public stance right now [on Huang’s possible return] is, “No, that’s not happening.” But Nvidia’s public stance a week and a half before that was, “We stand behind Jensen. We have every confidence in his leadership.”
So depending on the various pressures on them, you can imagine that changing. I don’t know what it would take for that to happen. I don’t necessarily think it’s that likely, but I also don’t think that just because they’re saying it’s not happening now doesn’t mean it will never happen.
Kirsten: Sure, never say never.
Tim: Right, never say never. I do think that to some extent, their steadfastness and how quickly they shot down the petitions asking for Jensen to return suggests there’s maybe a little bit more going on behind the scenes than we know on the outside. So that’s probably something to watch in the coming weeks.
Kirsten: I think that the board is trying to be in control here, and they don’t want to be forced into a decision because someone like Elon Musk is saying that it needs to happen. And so, even if there is a day in which Jensen returns — which I think is pretty unlikely, especially because the investigation into how much and who knew what about chips being sold, allegedly, secretly to China. We don’t know the full picture of that yet. But even if they did have the full picture, they want to present control, and they definitely don’t want to appear like they have deference to some other tech billionaire out there.
Tim: I’m sure they’re looking at what happened at OpenAI and not wanting to repeat that.

items.text:
Brazil’s Jair Bolsonaro in intensive care with bowel obstruction
The former president, serving a sentence for plotting a coup, is stable and breathing on his own, the hospital says.
Brazil’s former President Jair Bolsonaro is in intensive care after being diagnosed with an acute bowel obstruction, according to the DF Star hospital where he is being treated.
Bolsonaro, 71, was admitted on Friday with abdominal pain. In a bulletin on Saturday, the hospital said doctors have started giving him fluids and nutritional support, and inserted a tube into his stomach.
It said the former president is clinically stable and conscious, although they said there was no projected date for his discharge.
“There is hope that his condition will improve,” his son, Senator-elect Carlos Bolsonaro, wrote on X on Saturday afternoon. “He is being closely monitored and is fighting to get his bowels working again, with his usual grit and focus.”
In the early hours of Saturday morning, he described his father’s difficult night of treatment, where food residue was removed from his stomach using a tube inserted into his nose, and bouts of nausea.
“I’m not a doctor, but I’ve never seen him like this,” he wrote, suggesting that his father might need another surgery, which would be his 10th in less than eight years.
“All this is happening to a man sentenced to 27 years in prison without having committed any crime, while criminals do whatever they want with what’s left of this country,” the younger Bolsonaro continued.
Bolsonaro has been serving a 27-year sentence since last year for an attempted coup after losing the 2022 election to current President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. Bolsonaro has denied the charges.
He has been hospitalised repeatedly and has had to undergo surgeries after being stabbed in 2018 during a campaign event.
He was transferred in March to house arrest after spending several months in jail because of his health issues.
Next month, Brazil’s Supreme Court is set to consider the constitutionality of a law that changes how sentences are calculated, which could shorten his sentence and those of others convicted in the 2022 coup plot.

items.text:
Iran says held talks with Qatari mediators, urges US to accept conditions
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says reopening the strait is ‘not difficult’ if the US accepts reasonable conditions.
Iran says Qatari mediators have travelled to Tehran as the country’s foreign minister urges the United States to accept Iranian conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
News of the talks came as the commander of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) toured an underground missile facility on Saturday and the country’s president said Iran is facing a “silent economic war”.
A Qatari delegation visited Tehran on Friday night and held two hours of talks with Iranian officials, Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said, according to Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency.
“We are in contact with mediators, including the Qataris, both in person and virtually, and are holding the necessary discussions to see whether another opportunity can be given to diplomacy,” he said on Saturday.
The US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28, prompting Tehran to launch strikes against Israel and Gulf states hosting US military bases. The conflict has drawn in countries across the region, disrupted shipping and pushed up global energy prices.
Gharibabadi said the talks have not yet become formal negotiations. If they do, the technical details of Iran’s nuclear programme would be discussed, he added, but Iran’s position is that its enriched uranium must not leave the country.
He also said Iran regards the US economic blockade as an act of war and will “take any action necessary” to break it.
For his part, US President Donald Trump told Fox News on Saturday that he wants a “permanent” deal that stops Iran from getting a nuclear weapon. He said Iranian officials are “very, very difficult”.
“We make a deal, and then they break the deal the next day,” he added.
Reopening Hormuz ‘not difficult’
The ongoing talks in the region “must be given a chance, and the blockade must be lifted rationally,” Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Saturday, according to state television.
“Our position is clear: as long as Iran’s demands are not met, the discussion on the Strait of Hormuz and its opening is pointless,” he said.
“At the same time, we have always affirmed our readiness for dialogue, just as we are ready to defend ourselves.”
Iran’s conditions have included ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing Iranian assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending the US counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
Araghchi also said reopening the strait is “not difficult”, and requires the US only to “accept reasonable conditions that are in accordance with international law”, Tasnim reported.
The minister said there is “no solution” unless Washington acknowledges its mistakes and fulfils its previous commitments.
Iran has restricted shipping through the strait, which normally carried about a fifth of the world’s oil, since the war began. The US has imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports in response.
‘Silent economic war’
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Saturday that his country is facing a “silent economic war” that is “tougher than a war with missiles”, according to the state news agency IRNA.
Pezeshkian told a meeting of investors and producers that “a group of bullies, oppressors, and coercers sought to bring down our country”, but that Iranian businesses had managed market conditions well.
He said the government was working to avoid power cuts over the winter.
Meanwhile, IRGC commander Major-General Ahmad Vahidi toured an underground missile facility, accompanied by Brigadier General Majid Mousavi, who heads the IRGC Aerospace Force, Tasnim reported.
Vahidi was briefed on the force’s readiness and recent developments in its missile programme.
The visit follows the Aerospace Force’s unveiling of a new underground facility earlier this month, where it displayed ballistic and cruise missiles and their launchers, Tasnim said.

items.title: WSL roundup: Chelsea thwarted by Liverpool keeper, London City move to third
items.summary:
Khiara Keating’s resilient performance in goal denied Chelsea, the Women’s Super League leaders, and earned Liverpool a point, while London City Lionesses moved to within four points of the top by beating Crystal Palace 6-2.
After hard-fought 1-0 wins against Manchester City last Saturday and Paris
items.text:
Khiara Keating’s resilient performance in goal denied Chelsea, the Women’s Super League leaders, and earned Liverpool a point, while London City Lionesses moved to within four points of the top by beating Crystal Palace 6-2.
After hard-fought 1-0 wins against Manchester City last Saturday and Paris Saint-Germain on Wednesday night, Chelsea drew a blank. Against Gareth Taylor’s side, Chelsea’s lack of cutting edge was clear a week after they beat City to go top. The calf injury picked up by Melvine Malard against City, the absence of Lauren James, who has a thigh injury, and the form of Aggie Beever-Jones, who scored her first WSL goal in more than a year in the 6-0 defeat of Charlton, have left Chelsea’s attack short.
Despite almost 70% possession and 47 touches in the box to Liverpool’s 12, Sonia Bompastor’s side amassed only 19 shots to Liverpool’s 13 and seven on target to their opponents’ four. Although the Blues remain unbeaten in the WSL, their third draw in five games in all competitions means City can leapfrog them at the top if they beat Tottenham on Sunday.
Liverpool had chances, particularly in the first half, but were hanging on after the break and Keating helped them to a fourth clean sheet, a tally bettered only by Bompastor’s side.
“It was a bit stressful; we don’t want to sit back but in games like this you have to ride it out,” Keating told Sky Sports. “A clean sheet is always on our minds every game. We knew the mission. It was such a close game, it could have gone either way.”
The January transfer window will give the Blues an opportunity to strengthen their attack, but with three games before the winter break they need to step up in the final third, starting with their tricky fixture against London City Lionesses on 12 December after the international break.
London City came out on top in a thrilling end-to-end encounter with Palace. Having earned five of their nine points from losing positions this season, Palace did not cower when Eder Maestre’s team took the lead in Bromley. They twice came from behind to level the score before London City put the game beyond them.
The hosts had to weather some early Palace pressure, with Lexi Lloyd-Smith testing Elene Lete in the opening minute, with the goalkeeper starting in place of Mary Earps.
London City then took control and were rewarded in the 14th minute, when Daniëlle van de Donk turned in Isobel Goodwin’s cutback from close range. Palace were carved open, but they were not down and out against the team with ambitions of earning a place in next season’s Champions League.
Jo Potter’s side drew level via an Abbie Larkin volley into the bottom corner to stun the home team, with the visiting fans in full voice telling Alexia Putellas what she could do with her Ballons d’Or.
It felt fated that the three-time winner of the trophy would have the last laugh and within six minutes of the restart she restored her team’s lead, the ball falling kindly for her to turn into an empty net.
London City’s third came three minutes later and the scenario was similar. Shae Yañez failed to deal with a cross and Van de Donk swept it goalwards. Molly Bartrip was there to hook it away but the referee deemed it to have crossed the line.
The home team’s lead was cut to one in style by Palace when Fuka Tsunoda’s reverse pass was met by Annabel Blanchard and her side-footed volley looped over Lete and in. It was a stunning move and a stunning finish.
London City’s squad depth and fresh legs eventually helped them stretch the game beyond the stubborn visiting team, with Alanna Kennedy heading them back into a two-goal lead 15 minutes after coming on.
They killed the game off four minutes later, this time Goodwin rising highest to head in from another set piece, and Putellas put the cherry on top with her second at the death, looping the loose ball in after a big save from Yañez.
There were positives for Palace, despite remaining a precarious three points clear of Birmingham City, who play Manchester United on Sunday, but big-spending London City are just a cut above.

items.summary:
Eisenkot invites Netanyahu’s party for ‘marathon’ Israeli coalition talks
Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has invited caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party for coalition talks, his centrist Yashar party said Saturday. The "marathon series of talks" starts Sunda
items.text:
Eisenkot invites Netanyahu’s party for ‘marathon’ Israeli coalition talks
Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has invited caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party for coalition talks, his centrist Yashar party said Saturday. The "marathon series of talks" starts Sunday, the party said, adding that the move reflected a commitment to form "the broadest possible government" after the October election failed to deliver an outright winner.
Gadi Eisenkot, who is tasked with forming the next Israeli government, has invited the right-wing Likud party of caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu for coalition talks, his party said on Saturday.
Eisenkot's centrist Yashar party said the talks, scheduled to begin on Sunday, reflected a "genuine commitment to forming the broadest possible government".
Former military chief Eisenkot has until next month to form a government to replace Netanyahu, after the October election failed to deliver a clear majority for either bloc.
Read moreIsraeli opposition leader Eisenkot begins the hard work of forging a coalition government
Saturday's announcement comes as Eisenkot's wide-ranging anti-Netanyahu camp faces divisions on whether to forge alliances with the ultra-Orthodox parties and Arab-majority lists, or form a national unity government with Netanyahu's bloc.
"In an effort to pursue every option for forming a new government, Yashar Chair Gadi Eisenkot has instructed the party's negotiating team to invite its Likud counterparts to a marathon series of talks beginning with the meeting already scheduled for tomorrow (Sunday)," the party said in a statement.
It added that it would "leave no stone unturned as it works to make bold moves possible and secure the breakthrough needed to form a government".
Read more Netanyahu bloc targets Arab lawmakers as Israel's new parliament is sworn in
Former prime minister Naftali Bennett, an important figure in Eisenkot's camp, on Saturday called for a "Zionist unity government headed by Eisenkot" and said his party would refuse to join up with Netanyahu or his bloc.
In a statement, Bennett said he was "committed to ensuring that Netanyahu will not be the next Prime Minister of the State of Israel, and my party will not join him or his bloc under any circumstances", he added.
Netanyahu has been pushing hard for a national unity government, which he says is needed to guarantee Israel's security.
Eisenkot has indicated he would be open to forming a government with members of Netanyahu's Likud, but has previously ruled out serving in a government led by Netanyahu himself.
On Friday, Eisenkot vowed not to let coalition-building talks drag on and said that he would be prepared to put forward a minority national emergency government for a parliamentary vote should efforts to create a broad-based government fail.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

items.text:
Thousands protest across Europe over living costs and housing
Demonstrations in France and Portugal follow youth-led protests over education and economic hardship across Europe.
Thousands of people have taken to the streets across Europe to protest against rising living costs, unaffordable housing and cuts to public services, as students and workers demand action from their governments.
Demonstrators marched across France and Portugal on Saturday, following youth-led protests in several European countries on Friday.
The gatherings reflect overlapping concerns about economic insecurity, education and future opportunities, although their demands and scale differ considerably between countries.
In France, the Ministry of Interior said 82,500 people joined demonstrations nationwide on Saturday, including 21,500 in Paris, down from 106,000 the previous weekend. Organisers estimated a higher turnout of 150,000.
The protests, now in their sixth consecutive weekend, began in September with students demanding better schools before expanding to include trade unions and the Yellow Vests, a movement that emerged in 2018 over rising fuel prices and living costs.
Demonstrators have also criticised police violence and a new law strengthening protections for officers who use firearms.
Portugal protests
In Portugal, thousands marched through Lisbon despite heavy rain, calling for higher wages, affordable housing and relief from rising prices.
The demonstration was organised by CGTP, the country’s largest trade union federation, which also demanded higher pensions and cheaper essential goods.
Portugal’s housing pressures have intensified as property prices have more than doubled since 2017.
Average annual earnings in 2025 were 37 percent below the European Union average, according to the EU’s statistics agency, Eurostat.
The weekend’s demonstrations followed Friday’s youth protests in Germany and Sweden.
About 4,000 people gathered in Berlin, while police reported roughly 200 participants at a Saturday march in Helsinki organised by left-wing and student groups.
Organisers of an international youth strike said demonstrations were planned in at least 25 countries, with demands ranging from greater education funding and climate action to opposition to compulsory military service.
In Germany, the youth campaign Gen Z regelt, meaning “Generation Z takes charge”, announced demonstrations in 73 locations.
In Italy, a nationwide strike organised by the CGIL, one of the country’s main trade union confederations, disrupted transport, schools and some healthcare services on Friday.
Demonstrations took place in more than 100 cities, with union leader Maurizio Landini claiming more than one million participants nationwide.
While some protests were linked through the international youth initiative, others grew out of established national campaigns, bringing different groups onto the streets over concerns about living standards and government spending.
Separately, thousands protested in the Croatian capital, Zagreb, on Saturday over the death of a man at a psychiatric hospital.
Four medical technicians are under investigation on suspicion of aggravated murder.

The agrochemical and biotech giant Bayer has agreed to pay billions of dollars to people who sued the company alleging the weed-killer Roundup caused their cancer.
On Friday, a judge in Missouri gave final approval to the nationwi
items.text:
Bayer reaches Roundup settlement that could cost the company billions
The agrochemical and biotech giant Bayer has agreed to pay billions of dollars to people who sued the company alleging the weed-killer Roundup caused their cancer.
On Friday, a judge in Missouri gave final approval to the nationwide settlement that could cost the company up to $7.25 billion in the coming years.
The money will go to thousands of people who have been or will be diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma — a blood cancer that they claim is linked to glyphosate, which is the main ingredient in Roundup.
Under the settlement in circuit court, people affected could receive anywhere from $10,000 to $165,000 in compensation, depending on whether their work in agriculture or other occupations exposed them to higher levels of glyphosate, the age when they were diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma and other factors.
In a statement, the CEO of Bayer, Bill Anderson, called the settlement a "decisive milestone" that will "mitigate the risks" of pending and future litigation.
The presiding judge, Timothy Boyer, said it was "among the largest in the history of mass tort personal-injury class action settlements."
Earlier this year, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in favor of Bayer, the German company that now owns Monsanto, finding that it could be shielded from lawsuits filed in state courts over claims that it failed to warn consumers about the cancer-causing effects of glyphosate.
Roundup is the most widely used weed-killer in the world.
The attorney representing the plaintiffs, Christopher Seeger, said in a statement that "Today's final approval order delivers guaranteed compensation to Roundup cancer victims who have waited more than a decade for justice."
The latest settlement comes in addition to a previous one in which Bayer agreed to pay between about $10 billion and $11 billion to settle more than 100,000 claims related to Roundup.
More than a decade ago, the World Health Organization's cancer agency concluded that glyphosate is probably carcinogenic to humans. Prominent scientists in the field of environmental health have echoed those concerns as recently as this year.
But Bayer has steadfastly denied that its product causes cancer.
The Environmental Protection Agency has also concluded it "did not identify risks of concern from glyphosate uses, including for cancer," though the agency is currently conducting a review of the evidence related to human health after facing intense pressure from advocates and some scientists.
Concerns about the safety of glyphosate has been an animating issue for supporters of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr and his Make America Healthy Again agenda.
However, the Trump administration has taken steps to support the herbicide-maker, siding with Bayer in the Supreme Court case and issuing an executive order to promote domestic production of glyphosate.
Several years ago, the company removed glyphosate from its U.S. products used in residential settings, although it's still in use in the agricultural industry.

items.text:
Nations Championship fixtures: France to play South Africa in final as England face New Zealand rematch plus Ireland vs Australia
World Rugby's 12-team Nations Championship launched in 2026, uniting Six Nations sides, Rugby Championship teams, Fiji, Japan; tournament saw Tests in July, November before Finals Weekend at Twickenham Nov 27-29; France to face South Africa, England vs New Zealand, Ireland vs Australia
Saturday 21 November 2026 22:29, UK
South Africa will face France in the inaugural Nations Championship final at Allianz Stadium Twickenham on Sunday November 29, despite suffering back-to-back defeats.
The last round of regular fixtures for the tournament saw South Africa suffer defeat to Ireland in Dublin, a week on from losing to France in Paris, but owing to New Zealand losing to England at Twickenham - and failing to pick up any bonus points - the Springboks still finished top of the southern hemisphere table.
France defeated Argentina with a bonus point to confirm their place at the top of the northern hemisphere table ahead of England and Ireland.
The Nations Championship finals take place at Allianz Stadium Twickenham over from November 27-29.
Wherever each northern hemisphere nation finishes in their table decides who they will face next weekend, setting up Tests with the corresponding finishers in the southern hemisphere.
As a result, England will face New Zealand in a rematch on Saturday, while Ireland will play Australia on Friday night.
Fourth-placed Scotland will face Argentina on Sunday, fifth-placed Wales play Japan on Saturday, and sixth-placed Italy will face Fiji on Friday, having just lost to them in Udine.

England vs New Zealand (4.40pm kick-off)

Final: France vs South Africa (4.40pm kick-off)
What is it?
The Nations Championship is a joint venture between Six Nations and SANZAAR that pits the giants of northern and southern hemisphere rugby against each other on a more consistent basis.
The tournament is designed to align northern and southern hemisphere rugby calendars, guaranteeing high-profile fixtures to add more structure and meaning to the existing international windows between World Cups.
How does it work?
Each team will play six matches: three in July in the southern hemisphere and three in November in the northern hemisphere.
Twickenham's Allianz Stadium will then host Finals Weekend from November 27 to 29, where the inaugural champions will be crowned.
Rankings for Finals Weekend will be determined by results from the opening six matches, with each northern hemisphere team playing an additional fixture against the correspondingly ranked southern side.

items.title: How 'complacent' Arsenal unravelled at Newcastle - and their key lesson
items.summary:
Arsenal escape with 2-2 draw at Newcastle after 'complacent' second half almost proves costly for defending champions
Arsenal were completely dominant in the first half at Newcastle but saw their 1-0 lead turn into a 2-1 deficit before Noni Madueke rescued a point against their re-energised hosts; M
items.text:
Arsenal escape with 2-2 draw at Newcastle after 'complacent' second half almost proves costly for defending champions
Arsenal were completely dominant in the first half at Newcastle but saw their 1-0 lead turn into a 2-1 deficit before Noni Madueke rescued a point against their re-energised hosts; Mikel Arteta called the result "two points dropped" and revealed key lesson required to take "next step"
Saturday 21 November 2026 21:19, UK
From "exceptional" to "complacent" - Arsenal's drop-off in the second half at Newcastle was extraordinary.
Noni Madueke's equaliser at least rescued a point, but after completely dominating the first half at St James' Park Mikel Arteta says his team have learnt a harsh lesson about the need to deliver a complete performance in the Premier League.
Credit has to go to Newcastle, who were energised by Matthias Jaissle's triple substitution at half-time, with Tino Livramento, Jacob Ramsey and Anthony Elanga bringing intensity. Harvey Barnes and Malick Thiaw brought the goals. But the Premier League champions were their own worst enemy and, in the end, were fortunate to get away with their lead at the top of the table improved - for now.
With Man City dropping points again on Saturday and surprise-package Brighton still to play on Sunday, Arsenal remain firmly in the box seat. But Arteta is eager to drive even higher standards in his squad this season as he builds on last year's success - and he was far from impressed with how his team allowed Newcastle back into the game.
"My feeling is that we lost two points today," he told Sky Sports. "We were exceptional in the first half. At every level. Our intensity, the clarity that we have, how to attack the jumps of Newcastle every time they wanted to go man-to-man, the composure that we have, the way we use our relationship to break their press...
"It should have been 2-0, 3-0 or 4-0 up. But it wasn't. And when it wasn't, then we expected in the second half that we have to again raise the level because the opponent is going to have a reaction. The opponent did have a reaction and we were very below the level that is required to stretch the gap in a game like this in this stadium. And then we gave them belief.
"I say we give them belief because we give them a goal, we give them a throw-in that we just give them the ball. We have no structure to control the opposite winger. We concede a goal and it's game on.
"And from that it became a very chaotic game. Every set-piece, we know that they are exceptional at it and we concede from a set-piece.
"And then you have to react. Then we went back to the exceptional team that we were in the first half again for another 25 minutes and we scored a great goal. We create infinity of openings to create and score the third goal, but we lack some time or to be precise, to make that count."
The stats paint a clear picture of how different the two halves from Arsenal's perspective were. Attacking stats and, significantly, duel success numbers shifted.
Sky Sports pundit Jamie Redknapp said: "I think in the second half Arsenal were just complacent. I think they thought this was so easy and that can happen sometimes in a game.
"You're getting so much time on the ball. Declan Rice was able to turn. Bruno Guimaraes had so much time in the first half and then all of a sudden [Jacob] Ramsey comes on and he's all over you. He's closing you down. Myles Lewis-Skelly's getting under pressure and that was a full credit to Newcastle.
"The fundamentals that you have to do to win a football match by winning second balls, by putting teams under pressure, by getting in people's faces, Newcastle did well in the second half."
For former Arsenal striker Ian Wright, there is also an issue in the construction of Arsenal's midfield.
"What's worrying for me and probably for Arsenal fans is that that period where we seem to can't get it back, can't grasp it back," he said.

He added: "It was worrying to see Arsenal collapse like they did, for the time that they did."
An injury to goalkeeper David Raya presents another problem.
Goalscorer Madueke made a point of noting the "character" Arsenal showed to get back into the game after the turnaround from 1-0 to 2-1. On reasons for the poor start to the second half he said: "Not sticking by our own principles. I don't know whether we came out too relaxed after the first half performance."
The quality of that first half performance shouldn't be overlooked. Nor should Newcastle's role in changing the game.
But clearly Arteta will zone in on that second 45 and use it as an example of how he can raise further the levels of the English champions.
"I think individually we have some top performances for 70 minutes," said Arteta. "But at this level it's not enough. At this level requires 96 [minutes] unless you score three or four goals and then you can allow yourself for 15 or 20 minutes not to be at your best.

items.title: France’s sixth consecutive Saturday of protests draw lower turnout
items.summary:
France’s sixth consecutive Saturday of protests draw lower turnout
Turnout was down at largely peaceful demonstrations across France on the sixth consecutive Saturday of protests over the cost of living, with the interior ministry putting the figure at 82,500 across the country. Organisers said 150,
items.text:
France’s sixth consecutive Saturday of protests draw lower turnout
Turnout was down at largely peaceful demonstrations across France on the sixth consecutive Saturday of protests over the cost of living, with the interior ministry putting the figure at 82,500 across the country. Organisers said 150,000 people participated in the nationwide protests, down from their 200,000 figure last week.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Tens of thousands of people marched in cities in France on Saturday, on the sixth weekend in a row of protests to demand better public services and express anger over the rising cost of living and inequality.
The protest movement, sparked in mid-September by high school students demanding better learning conditions, fuelled a nationwide campaign against soaring prices, inadequate public services and police brutality that spread across Europe, even as turnout in France has dwindled.
Across the country, organisers reported 150,000 protesters, compared to 200,000 last week and 800,000 on the first one held October 17.
The interior ministry said numbers had "significantly declined", counting 82,500 people, compared to 106,000 last Saturday.
Read moreInterior ministry says 82,500 people protest across France, unions claim 150,000
Thousands of people gathered in central Paris's Place de la République square in a festive atmosphere, with musicians playing, food trucks, costumes and homemade signs, before marching east through the city.
Flags and vests of trade unions and left-wing parties mingled with those of student organisations and the Yellow Vest movement, which is marking its anniversary eight years after it rattled President Emmanuel Macron's government.
One group had set up mock headstones proclaiming the death of France's public services, including social security and education.
"In a number of countries, young people are going through the same thing, namely precarity. You have to choose between having a roof over your head, getting medical care, and being able to eat your fill," said Manon Moret, general secretary of the students' union Unef.
On Friday crowds rallied across multiple countries to vent anger over issues from high living costs to military spending and the climate crisis, ramping up pressure on political leaders they accuse of ignoring the concerns of young people.
"I want to live, not survive," read one placard held by a protester in Paris.
Police law
Another read: "No to the licence to kill", in reference to a law adopted by France's parliament on Friday increasing protection for law enforcement officers using their weapons, heavily criticised by the left.
The protests have been largely peaceful but have seen fringe violence and accusations of police brutality.
At least 31 people have been seriously injured by security forces since the protests began, according to a count by AFP based on direct testimonies, victims' lawyers and NGO records. Authorities have not provided an official toll.
Last month, some rallies across France degenerated into clashes between riot police and demonstrators, with shops looted and buildings attacked and torched.
Read moreLatest cost-of-living protests bring more than 140,000 onto the streets across France
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez had warned regional authorities to be "particularly vigilant regarding the groups most hostile to law enforcement" after the police law was adopted.
Vehicles burned
Protesters marched on Saturday in cities from Lille in the north to Marseille in the south and Lyon in the southeast.
Clashes broke out on the sidelines of some protests as people tried to rally in banned areas, set fire to vehicles and bins, with police firing tear gas.
Unions and activists have called for more protests in the coming weeks.
Avril Bas, who attended the Paris protest with her knitting group to support high school students' demands for better learning conditions, was not discouraged by the lower turnout on Saturday.
"If we take care of our young people, our students, we'll have a wonderful tomorrow and that's why I'm here," the 27-year-old told AFP.
"We'll be there next week and the next week and as long as we're needed," she said.

Why is the US Army detonating lead-rich explosives in Iowa?
The delayed blasts have stoked environmental fears and concerns about health effects in the state.
The United States Army is slated to conduct two controlled detonations at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in the Midwestern state of Iowa, aim
items.text:
Why is the US Army detonating lead-rich explosives in Iowa?
The delayed blasts have stoked environmental fears and concerns about health effects in the state.
The United States Army is slated to conduct two controlled detonations at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in the Midwestern state of Iowa, aiming to destroy 68 drums of degraded lead azide — a highly volatile, lead-based explosive used to trigger the main charges in some conventional munitions.
Announced just five days before an original Friday, November 20, detonation date, the Army’s decision was authorised by an emergency permit issued by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
Residents, environmental health experts, and Iowa elected officials have decried the detonation of lead-rich explosive material, citing scant public notice and potential environmental and health harms.
In a statement posted on X on Thursday, Iowa Democratic Senator-elect Josh Turek stressed the need for greater transparency.
“Iowans deserve to know that every safety precaution has been taken and exactly what the associated health risks are. Until those questions are answered, the detonation should not proceed,” he wrote.
Mounting public pressure has prompted the military to push the controlled blasts back to Monday, November 23.
But a late-stage legal challenge has cast doubt on whether the army will be able to proceed at all.
On the eve of the originally scheduled operation, two Iowa environmental advocacy groups — the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club’s Iowa chapter — petitioned a federal appeals court to overturn the EPA emergency permit, arguing that the agency had not given the public meaningful advance notice, failed to require adequate safeguards to protect human health and the environment, and sanctioned the operation without sufficient consideration of safer disposal alternatives.
Here’s what we know so far:
What is happening at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant?
In a November 15 advisory, the US Army warned residents of Middletown, a southeastern Iowa city of about 360 people, that the emergency blasts would loft a dust plume containing “some lead”, accompanied by loud explosions and ground vibrations.
The army’s containment strategy centres on thoroughly drenching the soil above the existing igloo-like, earth-covered concrete magazines — where the chemicals have been stored — with water before and during the detonations to help suppress airborne dust and particles.
The magazines are ringed by sand-filled barriers rising roughly two storeys high, designed to eject the force of the blast vertically into the sky, rather than laterally across the surrounding landscape.
“These measures should reduce the amount of lead that migrates from the detonation through the air off the installation,” the advisory reads.
According to the military’s modelling predictions, the blasts will deliver elevated airborne lead levels, but will remain “below the level at which EPA would require protective actions be taken”.
That’s reassurance with a blind spot, experts say.
Patrick O’Shaughnessy, an environmental health professor at the University of Iowa, who will be monitoring the environmental fallout from the detonations, says that for all the assumed precision of the army’s modelling, its most consequential variable remains undisclosed to the public: precisely how much lead each explosion will propel into the air.
It is the very quantity that will shape the scale of the downwind exposure.
“The unprecedented aspect of it is that normally in the world of air pollution, we have some estimation of what’s called the emission factor, the emission strength. We know how many pounds per second will be distributed out into the air from a smokestack,” O’Shaughnessy told Al Jazeera, “but in this case, we have no idea.”
The longer-term, more invisible peril, O’Shaughnessy said, is lead settling on playground equipment, getting into crops, landing in back yards and on other play surfaces where people could be exposed.
Why is the US Army detonating the explosives?
During a safety review in March, technicians discovered a stockpile of deteriorating lead azide that had languished in storage bunkers for 20 years at its Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, a sprawling 19,000-acre installation in Des Moines County, about 16 kilometres (10 miles) west of the Mississippi River, which separates Iowa and the state of Illinois.
Since then, the Army says it has engaged with the local community, including at an open house at the Army Reserve Center in mid-October for residents within a 50-mile (80km) radius of the facility, where it outlined its developing plans to eliminate the explosive hazard.
The stockpile includes roughly 9,700 pounds (just under five tonnes) of the explosives across 68 barrels, set to be detonated in place — material that contains roughly 6,900 pounds (about 3.5 tonnes) of lead by chemical mass.
During long-term storage, liquid in the drums evaporated and caused the lead azide to recrystallise.
According to the environmental assessment for Lead Azide Risk Mitigation, prepared by the Army, the recrystallisation had heightened the material’s sensitivity to shock and friction.
“Due to its chemical degradation, the material’s legal status transitioned from a viable production component to an unserviceable hazardous waste,” the report states.
Army Sustainment Command spokesperson Justine Barati said the Army faced a narrowing window to destroy the chemical material before colder weather or disturbances increased the risk of spontaneous detonation, which would pose an unacceptable risk of killing technicians on-site.
“We’re trying to do a controlled detonation to minimise the impact to the community and the environment. This is not something that we take lightly. We know that this is a disruption to people and that is not our intent, but we’re trying to do this in the safest manner possible,” Barati told a local television news station earlier this week.

items.summary: One of the items on the agenda for UN diplomats meeting in Geneva this week was working towards rules regarding the use of autonomous weapons, or so-called “killer robots.” Eventually, representatives left the meetings agreeing to “start discussing options” after a largely fruitless week of negotiat
items.text:
One of the items on the agenda for UN diplomats meeting in Geneva this week was working towards rules regarding the use of autonomous weapons, or so-called “killer robots.” Eventually, representatives left the meetings agreeing to “start discussing options” after a largely fruitless week of negotiations.
The UN fails to agree on rules regulating ‘killer robots’
Countries agree to ‘start discussing options’ for rules around autonomous weapons.
According to NPR:
Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. That call was backed by the U.N. secretary-general and by Pope Leo.
The compromise reached was that countries would instead have two years to propose regulations. Negotiations between countries on which regulations to adopt and how to enforce them will likely drag on well beyond that. Additionally, room was left for some of those yet-to-be-adopted regulations to remain “optional.”
Humanitarian organizations and some countries see a need to urgently adopt legally binding rules as semi-autonomous weapons and drones have been responsible for a significant number of civilian deaths in conflicts around the globe, including in Ukraine, Gaza, and Sudan.
According to NPR, Russia, Israel, and the US proved to be the primary obstructions:
On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting’s agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons.

items.title: Pochettino needs New Manager Bounce to break torrid Manchester United turnover | Jonathan Wilson
items.summary:
Everybody knows the pattern. Performances fade. Results falter. A title challenge becomes clinging on for the last Champions League spot becomes mid-table. Or a promising start becomes a troubling dip, becomes a full-on battle against relegation.
Fans begin to grumble. The media wonder whether the s
items.text:
Everybody knows the pattern. Performances fade. Results falter. A title challenge becomes clinging on for the last Champions League spot becomes mid-table. Or a promising start becomes a troubling dip, becomes a full-on battle against relegation.
Fans begin to grumble. The media wonder whether the spark has gone. Players look disaffected. A dressing room, once lost, is seldom rediscovered, and few managers are given the opportunity to find it again. A crisis in football, once acknowledged, is only ever resolved in one way: by the sacking of the manager.
With hindsight, Michael Carrick’s dismissal was probably inevitable from the moment Manchester United lost at Hull on the opening weekend, just as Ruben Amorim was doomed from the moment cameras picked him up fiddling with magnetic counters on a tactics board in the rain at Grimsby. The message for Mauricio Pochettino is clear: don’t go playing badly on the east coast.
It’s generally acknowledged that Carrick, while he may not have been the ideal manager for United, was a long way down the list of the biggest problems at the club. So what was the point of sacking him? As Pochettino begins his United career at Anfield on Sunday, what realistically can any manager hope to achieve?
Sackings have become almost ritualistic. Football demands blood sacrifice. How else can the harvest be guaranteed but by the torching of the wicker man? How else can Crystal Palace stay up but by the sacking of Pierre Sage? Once, when the manager defined the club, bought the players, decided the tactics, set the mood, that perhaps made sense. When managers were messiahs, it requires only a slight tweak to the underlying theology to see a logic in sacrificing them.
But managers now, at least at the majority of Premier League clubs, are part of a wider structure. In one of his meltdowns at Spurs, Antonio Conte made the point that it made little sense for him to be answering questions about the broader future of the club when he had so little power compared with the tiers of executives. Why sack the manager rather than the head of recruitment or the sporting director or the chair?
The answer to that perhaps goes back to the emergence of the English idea of the manager, which began in the 1930s and blossomed in the post-war golden age of Matt Busby, Bill Shankly, Don Revie and Brian Clough. As Barney Ronay argues in The Manager, at least part of the reason he became a figure of such pre-eminence was that it was useful for the board to have a hapless ashen-faced figure standing out on the touchline to take the blame. A handful of geniuses aside, the manager was essentially a convenient scapegoat.
But does the sacrifice work? It was one of the shibboleths of football’s early data wonks that the new manager bounce was a myth. What was being witnessed when form improved after a sacking was nothing more than regression to the mean. Which sounds sensible: squads make games and are determined by finance. There is a wealth of evidence that the biggest single factor in determining league position is the wage bill.
And yet there is also evidence that new manager bounce does exist. A lot of early data analysis in football ignored the fact that those involved are human and respond emotionally to circumstance. More recent studies, though, suggest that, while around a quarter of clubs experience no improvement, the first five matches under a new manager show a 41% improvement in points per game, although the impact wears off after around 10 games.
That feels intuitively true and is readily explicable. A manager under pressure can become embattled, lashing out at enemies real and imagined, their capacity to make lucid decisions impaired as confidence ebbs, creating a doom spiral. Replacing him breaks that pattern and permits a psychological reset.
In a world where everything is studied endlessly, a new manager should make a team less predictable. It’s possible, of course, that as those early analyses suggested, performances would have turned anyway as part of a regression to the mean, but it is curious how often the uptick in form coincides with the replacement of the manager.
Anthropologists are yet to determine precisely why United sacrifice managers so frequently, although there does appear to be some sense of deflecting blame. There is also a sense that it has become routine, that reasons that once probably did exist have been forgotten over time.
Sacking the manager is just what the club do a few months into the season, the ritual now as divorced from its original purpose as modern Hallowe’en customs are from their origins in the Christian commemoration of All Hallows’ Eve.
Will the arrival of Pochettino help? He is a far more ebullient and charismatic figure than Carrick, whose status as a dead man walking for most of this season perhaps meant players did not take him as seriously as they might have an incumbent who appeared to be there for the long term, or had them beginning to ponder moves away from United.
But this remains a mismatched hotchpotch of a squad assembled over six previous managers. If there is some style of play that would suit most of them it has yet to reveal itself.
It will take time for Pochettino to instil in a side that are habitually outrun the levels of conditioning that characterised his Tottenham, and perhaps even longer to get them playing in a coherent pattern. There will probably have to be five or six new signings (and at least as many departures). Probably most difficult of all, there is the entire culture of the club to overhaul, which may not be possible without a change of ownership.
Given United came back from two goals behind three times in their final two games under Carrick, these are not usual circumstances: beleaguered managers rarely inspire such defiance, and the fans never turned against him. In that sense, there will not be the immediate benefit that comes when toxicity is removed.

items.text:
Russia attacks Zelensky's hometown, Ukraine reaffirms wish to join NATO
A Russian ballistic missile attack on President Volodymyr Zelensky’s hometown in central Ukraine on Saturday killed two people and wounded dozens. Hours later, Zelensky reiterated his country's determination to join NATO, following proposals to provide Kyiv with security guarantees similar to those of the military alliance.

A Russian strike on the center of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s hometown, Kryvyi Rih, killed two people and wounded 60 others, local officials said Saturday.
Meanwhile, a Russian cargo ship bound for Kaliningrad caught fire in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday after it was hit by drones, Finnish and Russian officials said. It was not clear who struck the ship not far from the Russian border. The Finnish prime minister warned that the war was spilling into the region.
Read moreDrone attack sets Russian cargo ship ablaze in Gulf of Finland
A 7-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman were killed in the attack Friday night on Kryvyi Rih in central Ukraine, Oleksandr Vilkul, the head of the city administration, wrote on Telegram. Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the regional military administration, said 60 people were wounded, including six children.
The strike caused four fires and damaged about 25 apartment buildings, a hospital, schools and an industrial facility, as well as businesses and vehicles, Vilkul said.
Video footage published by the regional branch of the Ukrainian State Emergency Service appeared to show further strikes while ambulance and firefighting crews were responding at the scene, as fires burned around them.
“First, two ballistic missiles. And then, when the emergency and rescue operation began, three more rockets hit doctors, rescuers and utility workers,” Vilkul wrote on Telegram.
The attack added to uncertainty about the prospects for ongoing talks brokered by Washington. It also came hours after two Russian missiles and a suspected drone came down in Poland, in what its prime minister said was likely a provocation timed to coincide with European military exercises in his country.
In the unprecedented two-week military exercise that began November 9 in southeastern Poland, forces are preparing for a possible postwar mission in Ukraine aimed at helping to stabilize the country and rebuild its military. European countries previously have expressed alarm at what they deem to be Russia’s attempts to destabilize the continent.
NATO will defend every inch of Polish territory, Rutte says
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, speaking to reporters in Warsaw on Saturday, called the airspace violation “dangerous” and said all allies stood “in full solidarity with Poland.”
“NATO will defend every inch of Polish territory,” Rutte said. He said the alliance functioned “as it should” on Friday morning, when NATO jets supported Polish F-16s scrambled as Russian objects approached Polish airspace. NATO’s top military commander was assessing the alliance’s defenses and would make adjustments if needed, Rutte said.
The head of NATO forces in Europe, General Alexus Grynkewich, would do everything necessary to identify any threats to defense and deterrence capabilities and would implement appropriate adjustments if needed, Rutte said.
On Monday, a meeting of NATO's North Atlantic Council will be held in Brussels to discuss the violation of Polish airspace by Russian missiles, PAP also reported on Saturday.
"In the near future, we will receive strong support from our NATO allies to bolster the protection of our eastern border," Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote on X on Saturday, commenting on the meeting of the NATO body.
"I've been in contact today with general Grynkewich, to coordinate the details of these measures."
Zelensky reaffirms Ukraine's wish to join NATO
Zelensky on Saturday reiterated his country's determination to join NATO, following proposals to provide Kyiv with security guarantees similar to those of the military alliance.
"Of course Ukraine very much wants to be in NATO," Zelensky told reporters, judging that membership of the alliance was one of the "most obvious security guarantees" for his country.
The issue of Ukraine joining NATO, ruled out by Washington since 2025, resurfaced in recent days during fresh talks to end the war nearly five years after Russia's invasion.
At a meeting with Kyiv's allies in Berlin on Thursday, US envoy Jared Kushner said Washington could be ready to grant Ukraine a security guarantee similar to that provided under Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty.
That clause -- the cornerstone of NATO -- states that an attack on one member is considered an attack on all allies.
Putin 'doesn’t want to stop the war'
At a meeting with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting in Kyiv, Zelensky said Saturday that Ukraine’s repeated attacks on the Kerch Bridge linking occupied Crimea with the Russian mainland were a “fair response” to scores of Russian attacks on Ukrainian bridges. He said that Russia President Vladimir Putin had "attacked Ukrainian bridges 109 times.”
“Not the number of missiles — the number of attacks,” he said. “This is important, that’s why it’s our absolutely fair response.”
The Ukrainian leader said Putin “doesn’t want to stop the war” and is looking to escalate. He also rejected Putin’s claim that the Kerch bridge is used exclusively by civilian traffic.
“If he can use internet, he can use it and see tanks, armored vehicles, artillery,” the Ukrainian leader said.

League leaders Arsenal miss the chance to go eight points clear of second placed Brighton, who play on Sunday.
Arsenal missed the chance to open up an eight-point lead at the top of the Premier League after a stirring second-
items.text:
Noni Madueke salvages draw for Arsenal at Newcastle United as Raya injured
League leaders Arsenal miss the chance to go eight points clear of second placed Brighton, who play on Sunday.
Arsenal missed the chance to open up an eight-point lead at the top of the Premier League after a stirring second-half fightback from Newcastle held the defending champions to a 2-2 draw.
The Gunners led on Saturday through Eberechi Eze’s strike after a dominant first 45 minutes.
But Mikel Arteta’s men were suddenly headed for defeat when goals from Harvey Barnes and Malick Thiaw provided a much-needed boost for under-fire Newcastle boss Matthias Jaissle.
Noni Madueke salvaged a point for Arsenal and stretched their lead at the top over surprise package Brighton to six points.
However, the loss of influential goalkeeper David Raya to injury could provide a twist in the title race that many believed Arsenal would cruise.
Newcastle remain in the bottom half of the table with just one win in six games in all competitions.
Yet, Jaissle can point to his side’s second-half performance as a potential turning point after a difficult start to his reign at St James’ Park.
Arsenal move back six points clear of third-placed Manchester City, but missed the chance to put their foot down in the defence of their title.
Madueke continued his impressive form in the injury absence of Bukayo Saka and hit the post early on.
Former Newcastle captain Bruno Guimaraes was roundly booed on his first return to Tyneside since making a 75 million pound ($98m) move to the Emirates Stadium in August.
The Brazilian nearly silenced his former faithful when he prodded just wide from a Madueke cross as Arsenal pressed for the opener.
It duly arrived 10 minutes before the break when Kai Havertz pounced on a poor touch by Lewis Hall and brilliantly played in Eze to blast high past Lukas Hornicek.
Jaissle got the response he needed from his half-time team talk as Newcastle came out a completely different proposition after the break.
Arsenal also played a part in letting the home side back into the game and lifting the 50,000 crowd in doing so.
Martin Odegaard shanked his attempt at a long ball forward to allow William Osula to play in Barnes to level.
Suddenly, an Arsenal side that had kept seven clean sheets in their opening 10 league games was on the rocks.
Thiaw bundled home a second for Newcastle just 13 minutes later after Dan Burn was left completely unmarked from a corner and his header was only parried by Raya.
That proved to be one of Raya’s final interventions as the Spaniard had to be replaced by Kepa Arrizabalaga.
Raya would be a massive miss if the Spaniard is sidelined for a significant spell.
But Arsenal regained their composure in time to salvage a point that keeps them well in the driving seat to retain the title.
Odegaard made amends for his earlier error by freeing Madueke down the righ,t and he cut inside before his tame deflected shot found a way past Hornicek.
Madueke told Sky Sports that he thought 2-2 was a “fair” result.
“Game of two halves is fair. First half we were outstanding. Should have got three goals, to be honest. Missed a couple of chances myself. Everything else was there,” he said.
“The second half, the first 20 minutes, was not good by our standard. When you give this team and crowd belief at home, it is difficult. We showed character to get back in the game, but 2-2 is a fair result.”

items.text:
If Mikel Arteta was delighted to see the back of Eddie Howe as Newcastle’s head coach, the bad news is that another similarly awkward technical area adversary has been installed at St James’ Park.
If Arsenal’s manager never seemed to relish trips to face Howe’s old team, Arteta certainly did not enjoy this latest trip to Tyneside where Matthias Jaissle’s initially overwhelmed team fought back to earn a point courtesy of a stellar second-half performance.
At half-time the crowd had felt close to turning against Jaissle but he held his nerve and, thanks to a triple substitution and smart tactical rejig suggested that he is no mug after all.
It left Arsenal – who lost their goalkeeper David Raya to a potentially significant second-half shoulder injury – still top of the Premier League, six points clear of Brighton and Manchester City and Arteta with a face like thunder.
Only last week Bruno Guimarães claimed he was “beloved” by Newcastle fans but the club’a former captain turned Arsenal midfielder found himself serenaded by a soundtrack of boos of the sort usually reserved for Sunderland players.
Newcastle’s problem is that, despite spending an awful lot of money, they have struggled to replace last season’s now departed star trio – Guimarães, Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon.
That reality perhaps left Howe’s successor making a not so subtle point with his team sheet here.
Of Jaissle’s starting XI only the goalkeeper, Lukas Hornicek, the right-back Amar Dedic and the midfielder Sean Steur were signed this summer.
The other five new faces that arrived during a close season that saw a total of around £275m invested on newcomers were either benched (Nico González and Matias Fernandez-Pardo) or did not make the 20-man match day squad (Aladji Bamba and Bazoumana Touré). Admittedly Ewen Jaouen is injured but, given that Bamba and Touré cost a combined £78.5m their total omission represented quite a statement. Ditto the decision to leave González and Fernandez-Pardo and their individual £50m plus price tags on the bench.
Back on the pitch the jury remained out on Hornicek. The Czech international has made some excellent saves this season but, here, his kicking proved pretty much uniformly poor and he was fortunate to be reprieved when he hesitated too long as the impressive Kai Harvertz closed in.
Jaissle’s technical frustration with his goalkeeper proved well apparent as Arsenal took increasing control of a first half that saw Newcastle’s lone striker, William Osula isolated and even their normally imperious England left back Lewis-Hall, given a thorough workout by Noni Madueke.
Much to Arteta’s chagrin, Lewis Miley, preferred to González in the midfield holding role, did his very best to slow the tempo but ultimately it proved a forlorn task. The red tide could only be stemmed for so long.
When Havertz dispossessed Hall in the wake of the latter miscontrolling a long ball, he cut inside and slid a highly intelligent, beautifully calibrated, pass across to the on-rushing Eberechi Eze. Without breaking stride, Eze exhibited perfect balance unleashed a gorgeous first-time shot that arrowed, inexorably, passed the powerless Hornicek.
As the home fans fell eerily silent, Arteta and his staff celebrated a goal sufficiently special to rebuke suggestions that his side are all about efficiency at the expense of artistry these days.
Given that on those rare moments when Newcastle’s attack looked as if it might flicker into life, Declan Rice always seemed on hand to reinforce his defence and smother any sort of danger, the omens were not bright for Jaissle.
Indeed it was a struggle to recall his side making a meaningful attacking touch inside Arsenal’s box and fans stationed near the home dugouts made their feelings plain to the manager.
Arsenal’s pressing was so good that Newcastle were left seemingly incapable of playing short passes and, instead found themselves reduced to aimless long balls. With Rice and Martin Ødegaard apparently operating on a different midfield planet an equaliser felt like a distant dream.
Yet however far fetched that vision was something Harvey Barnes would prove fully capable of buying into. The left winger is Newcastle’s best finisher. And when, early in the second half, Ødegaard made an uncharacteristic error, his heavy touch sliced the ball in Osula’s direction.
Once the Dane played it into the path of Barnes in it took a single, steadying, touch and an assured finish to leave the hitherto redundant David Raya picking his shot out of the net.
Jaissle’s introduction of Tino Livramento, Jacob Ramsey and Anthony Elanga - who, incidentally, were all at Newcastle last season - at the expense of Dedic, Steur and Jacob Murphy at the interval was. paying dividends. Suddenly, almost astonishingly, Arsenal were the team in danger of being pressed into submission.
The home side had begun closing their guests down far higher up the pitch and, along the way had morphed into an infinitely more menacing team.
Soon, they were ahead in the wake of a Hall corner headed down by Dan Burn, allowing Malick Thiaw to stab the ball beyond Raya.
Shortly afterwards Arsenal’s goalkeeper was helped off the pitch in evident pain after sustaining a nasty looking left shoulder injury during an ostensibly benign collision with Osula. On came Kepa Arrizabalaga in a triple substitution also featuring the withdrawl of Guimarães.
Madueke though was still around and he reminded everyone of his presence by meeting the counter-attacking Ødegaard’s stellar pass, dummying a couple of defenders and watching his slightly deflected shot evade Hornicek’s grasp.

Arsenal and Newcastle played out an entertaining 2-2 draw at St James' Park on Saturday.
The Gunners took the lead through Eberechi Eze in the first half before Harvey Barnes equalised after the break.
The hosts went ahead when Malick Thiaw bundled in from a corner before Noni Madueke brought the Gunners level with an excellent strike, and that is how it finished.
BBC Sport's Alex Howell has rated the players - and you can have your say too.

Newcastle United
Lukas Hornicek: His kicking was slightly erratic. Nearly got caught on the ball by Kai Havertz after taking too long to release it. Could have done better with the second Arsenal goal. 5
Amar Dedic: Booked after pulling back Eberechi Eze and had a tough evening against the England forward. 5
Malick Thiaw: Scored the goal to put Newcastle in front, which capped an excellent performance in central defence. 8
Dan Burn: Some crucial clearances in the first half and played a big part as Newcastle took the lead. 7
Lewis Hall: A big error for the opening goal when he failed to deal with a clipped ball over the top. The left back redeemed himself with a crucial block to deny Noni Madueke and provided some excellent deliveries into the Arsenal box. 7

Jacob Murphy: An early shot and tried to catch David Raya off his line, but also taken off at the break after a quiet first half. 5
Joe Willock: An all-action performance and his physicality was a big reason why Newcastle improved in the second half. 7
