items.text:
Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person.
You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later.
While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space.
Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work.
Ask Proxy
Ask Proxy’s biggest differentiator is that it “thinks like a woman,” meaning it aims to anticipate your needs before you even ask, the company explains on its website.
It works like a chatbot you can text like a friend, whether you need gift ideas, help planning an event, or recommendations for things to do that weekend. You can ask it to add important dates to your calendar, set reminders, or help with everyday decisions. You can also send it photos, like an empty table, to figure out how to decorate the table for a dinner party.
Unlike a typical chatbot, Ask Proxy also takes a proactive approach. It can reach out when it notices something you might forget or when it comes across a new activity, restaurant, or experience you might enjoy.
There’s also a work-focused version, which the company explains “gets employees back to work faster, while keeping personal data off company systems.”
The personal version costs $1 per day. For businesses, pricing starts at $15 per employee per month for large companies and $23 per employee per month for small teams with fewer than 49 employees.
Ask Proxy works over SMS. You can text “start” to 820-732-2625.
Caddy
Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check.
For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you.
Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026.
Comma
Comma is designed to manage tasks across both work and everyday life. Comma carries tasks through to completion, checking its own work and determining when a task is finished.
Completed work is surfaced for review when a decision or approval is needed. It also proactively notifies users and recommends the next steps.
It can work across a user’s browser, computer, and files, while remaining accessible remotely through messaging apps such as Signal, Telegram, and WeChat. Comma maintains context and memory across devices and conversations, and can deliver daily briefings, flag urgent matters, and summarize recorded calls.
Comma is free to start and open source.
Fambot
Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan.
The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar.
Fambot currently connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp, with support for Apple Calendar planned for the future.
The company launched in beta in early September 2026 and has raised $3.5 million in pre-seed funding. The service is currently free during the beta period, but Fambot expects to eventually charge roughly the equivalent of a Netflix subscription.
Folk
Folk is designed to be an AI assistant you can reach through iMessage, WhatsApp, and Telegram. It can remember personal context, manage reminders, research topics, track flights, handle email, and perform real-world tasks such as restaurant reservations.
One distinction is that Folk runs on its own private cloud computer. It can also run code and execute multi-step tasks rather than merely responding conversationally.
Folk launched its beta in May 2026, and it’s available for free but also offers a Pro subscription for $8.33/month if you want unlimited tasks running in the background.
Haven
Haven distinguishes itself by presenting the concept of a “digital twin” rather than merely serving as a text-based AI assistant.
According to the company, Haven understands and adapts to your preferences, routines, and decision-making styles, creating a personalized memory graph based on your interactions. As the company describes, “A personal assistant knows what you asked it to do. Haven knows what you would do and how you would do it.”
Notably, the company envisions future features that customize your experiences across devices, like TV and car.
Currently, Haven is available for free in beta on iPhone and Android devices, and the web. You can also reach Haven by calling or texting (435) 260-6500.
Instinct

items.title: Is selling an AI version of your face to this microdrama startup the future of Hollywood?

items.text:
For the most part, the content offered by the microdrama startup Shortical is indistinguishable from the rest of its industry. The company produces soapy, melodramatic storylines — almost always risqué romances — that, in bite-sized two-minute episodes, compel viewers to stay glued to their phones so as not to miss the latest twist in a tawdry, cliff-hanger-happy saga.
The primary way that Shortical — which was founded last January — makes money is through subscriptions. Typically, the first 7-10 episodes of a micro-drama are free. After that, if the user wants to finish the series, they have to pay a small monthly fee which unlocks access to all of the site’s content.
Over the past year, the company has churned out a gush of popular live-action romances like “Crossing the Line with My Neighbor,” “Accidentally Married My Boss,” and “Spoiled by My Billionaire Sugar Daddy.”
Lately, however, the company’s homepage is covered in AI-generated content. The reason isn’t exactly hard to figure out: the production overhead for AI content is substantially less than live-action. The profit potential, meanwhile, is substantially higher, if you can draw an audience.
Its latest microdrama premiered in Los Angeles last week. The series, called “Inevitable,” stars Aki Avni, an Israeli film and television star who has been visible in American TV shows for years (he had a stint on Fox’s 9/11-era thriller “24” years ago) but is now trying something largely unheard of in modern Hollywood: licensing his face to Shortical for the sake of its AI content.
The project, which is wholly AI, used Avni’s face to create a digital avatar of him. In “Inevitable,” he plays himself – in a very meta plot in which he — the actor Aki Avni — licenses his face to a film studio, after which thriller-like antics ensue.
This is Shortical’s first foray into such a licensing deal, but it likely won’t be their last.
In a phone interview, Avni told TechCrunch that he found the project both nerveracking and exciting. “Look, it’s a new era for artists,” the actor said. “AI is a new kind of art. It’s a new format. It’s always great to be the pioneer in something.”
Guy Shimoni, the CEO of Shortical, emphasized the creative potential of the new tool. “One of the things that AI does is it enables smaller teams to be able to produce these movie-scale productions,” Shimoni said. “When we were doing mobile-first live action, we were limited by budget, but now we can serve them with epic fantasies. We have kingdoms and dragons. We have superheroes. We have werewolves.”
But AI-generated romances involving werewolves — who, exactly, is watching this kind of thing?
Apparently, a lot of people. While China boasts the biggest microdrama audience globally, Shimoni says that most of his platform’s viewers are actually in the U.S. The industry’s viewer demographic skews heavily female. Many viewers may watch them to wind down at night, getting minor dopamine hits as they drift off to sleep. Many of the AI-generated programs that already exist on the company’s website appear to have millions of views.
Now, Shortical is betting on the creation of a new generation of creators — those who, like Avni, are willing to surrender their likenesses for compensation. “LICENSE YOUR FACE” Shortical’s website advertises, explaining that interested parties can submit their social media handles to the company, which will then decide whether to offer them “a contract setting out the terms” of using their persona in the company’s AI-generated content.
A company rep told TechCrunch that this “offering is still in its early days and hasn’t yet resulted in any signed contracts.” They added: “The series with Aki is the first time Shortical has used a real person’s likeness, and it was done through a direct agreement with him rather than through the platform. Shortical hopes the series will draw more attention to face licensing and plans to promote the offering more actively following this launch.”
Much of this trend has already taken hold in China where the microdrama industry originated, where AI-generated content is big, and where face-licensing is already a trend. Although the trend may not be a particularly profitable one for creators. A recent report in Rest of World found that Microdrama firms were paying people “between US$15 to US$700 to license their facial likenesses.”
How much money is Shortical offering for its face-licensing deals? The company isn’t saying. As for if Shortical will offer royalty-based compensation for creators — like the residual system in television, “It’s a case by case [basis],” Shimoni answers vaguely.
A Shortical representative further explained to TechCrunch that the company didn’t want to “share a specific figure” for Avni’s particular contract. However, the person said, he came “on as a partner in the project, and his compensation was in line with industry standards for a comparable non-AI acting role.”
For other actors, however, the deals may be quite different. Plus, many creatives are understandably unsettled by signs of automation creeping into their industry. Until recently, microdramas seemed like a safe, entry-level gateway into the entertainment industry, where young actors could gain experience on sets and hone their craft. Now, companies are downsizing and producing content that doesn’t even require real actors.
Jennifer Cooper, a longtime fan of the industry and founder of the consultancy firm Vertical Drama Love, notes that there’s a lot of distrust of AI — both from audiences and within the microdrama industry itself.
“Everyone’s been impacted by AI,” she said. “A lot of us have either lost work to AI or can see that it’s devastated this industry — [taking microdramas] from something that was a rare thing in the world, that was in growth, and providing work, particularly for young people…[and now] you know, it’s been decimated.”

items.text:
Today, I’m talking with Hayden Field, The Verge’s senior AI reporter, about the Anthropic IPO for the third and final episode in our series about AI in real life.
Can Anthropic afford to put safety first?
The Anthropic IPO raises big questions about the future of AI, the company’s safety-first mission, and how we balance idealism with capitalism.
The AI lab behind Claude went public on the Nasdaq last Thursday. The numbers are gigantic, but not really that important for this conversation, except to say that Anthropic has become one of the most valuable companies on the planet.
The real story is what happens now — and whether Anthropic can continue to thread the needle of caring about and investing in AI safety while also being a public company beholden to shareholders. Oh, and it also continuously growing the amount of money it makes so it can keep paying its ever-increasing compute bills, which total roughly $900 billion over the coming years.
All of these ideas sit in a fascinating tension with one another, and so Hayden and I really tried to break down how we think this might play out as Anthropic navigates the pressures of the public markets.
You’ll hear us talk about the company’s unique corporate governance structure, something that is especially relevant in the wake of the ongoing Jensen Huang saga. We also get into why OpenAI seems happy to have let Anthropic go public first, and why Anthropic’s whole pitch to big customers boils down to the same safety branding that now sits in conflict with the profit-oriented part of its business.
Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.
Okay: Hayden Field, The Verge’s senior AI reporter, on the Anthropic IPO and the economics of frontier AI. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Hayden Field, welcome back to Decoder.
Thanks. Great to be here.
I’m excited to talk to you today because it’s not pure soap opera drama chaos.
I know.
It’s like a normal thing that happened.
It’s for once not personality-based and soap opera. It’s about cold, hard would-be cash.
[Laughs] Well, there is some personality in it because we’re going to talk a lot about Anthropic’s IPO, which has a bunch of big personalities in it, and the way they have structured this company to repel the rapacious pressures of capitalism is, I would say, very eccentric. It reflects the beliefs of a number of eccentric people.
Yep, absolutely. It’s really been interesting digging into the S-1 again and just seeing who was on what committee and which founders have the most control here and how much control the founders actually have, which is more than it may seem.
Let’s start at the start. You and I are talking on IPO day. Anthropic is the first pure AI lab to go public. They priced the IPO at $83 a share and they got all the way up to $111. By the time people are listening to this, who knows what the price will actually be, but it’s been a real victory lap for all the people who are invested in Anthropic. A bunch of law firms have changed their homepages to be like, “Congratulations, guys!”
What do you make of this? Is it just the thing that had to happen or is it a sign that the AI bubble is not going to pop? How should people think about it?
I don’t think it really gives us new information about whether the AI bubble is going to pop or not, because I mean, this is peak AI hype right here. It’s the first AI lab to go public. It’s been kind of on track to break records for months. Everyone was like, “It’s probably going to beat Musk,” and then it did. I can’t wait to see his tweets later.
But the other interesting part of this is that I’ve heard thousands of new millionaires and hundreds of new centimillionaires will be born from this, not to mention billionaires, too. It’s one of those things where I think the AI bubble is continuing to swell.
I was even chatting with some tech workers inside a bunch of different companies this morning, and they were all saying within their companies, they’re seeing the bubble swell and swell, and they’re being tasked with doing more and more AI, even if it makes them less productive and makes the work less good.
So I think there’s going to be a reckoning eventually, but right now we’re at peak AI hype and Anthropic does a great job of marketing its business as safe AI. Of course, they’re going to have more pressure around that marketing term now more than ever. So it’s going to be interesting to see the tension point kind of go into the spotlight and see how they handle this.
Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.
I was at the Semafor conference earlier this week. I saw Sam Altman and Sarah Friar, OpenAI’s CFO, on stage there. Altman and Greg Brockman were at the DealBook conference this week. I get the sense they’re kind of happy that Anthropic went first to see what happens in the markets and to see how companies value the revenue potential of their big competitors so they can tell their IPO story better.
Is that the sense you get, that Anthropic is the trial balloon? Or is OpenAI just retconning the fact that it didn’t go first?
Yes, I think that’s absolutely the case. I heard there was a time in the past year that Altman was really obsessed with beating Anthropic to go public. That’s what I heard. It was all he thought about. But then with all the bad press around OpenAI this year, they’ve had setback after setback. A lot of the public is particularly focused on hating OpenAI right now.
Obviously, there’s a big AI populism backlash and a lot of people hate a lot of AI, but it seems like OpenAI has really borne the brunt of a lot of public hatred and scandals this year. And so they were like, “You know what? Let’s just take a step back and let Anthropic go first.” And they seem happy to do that.

items.text:
Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis
Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis
Joint statement by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative.
On November 20, 2026, Levent Alpöge released a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as a Lean library comprising 17 million lines of code.
We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement.
Our rationale is outlined below.
The codebase depends directly only on Mathlib. Over the past day, part of the Lean and Mathlib communities have rallied to verify the proof's correctness. We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct. The four criteria in https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2026/11/12/and-the-proof-is-checked-in-lean/ are all satisfied.
- The statement of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct. This statement is part of Mathlib: RiemannHypothesis and has been carefully vetted by experts in Lean and number theory.
- Alpöge’s library compiles correctly. By now, dozens of people have reported correct compilation of the codebase, reproducing the same raw proof export file. The library compiles without errors or build failures.
- 
The code proves the correct statement. Crucially, the community has added a file that isolates the statement of the Riemann Hypothesis and imports only Mathlib. That statement was compared against the theorem proved by Alpöge using two independent tools (comparator and con-leche –compare), both confirming that the theorem proved in Alpöge’s library is exactly Mathlib’s statement of the Riemann Hypothesis.
- 
The Lean proof is valid. The exported raw proof has been checked by several proof checkers, including Lean’s official kernel, the con-leche and con-ron checkers, and several independent checkers contributed by third parties and implemented in different programming languages. The checkers con-leche and con-ron come with a formal proof, relative to set theory, that they cannot accept a false proof, thus addressing concerns that Lean’s logic itself might have flaws that the proof could exploit. An extensive overview is available at https://math.mit.edu/~drew/grh/. These checks ran on an inert export of the proof, out of reach of hypothetical malicious code in the Lean proof sources.
Thanks are owed to everyone in the community who provided resources for the verification.
We look forward to all the activity in the mathematical community that will help explain the new ideas in this proof.

items.text:
Chess.com is ready to go a lot bigger than chess. After launching Gambit, a gambling-free poker site, earlier this year, the company is now adding 10 more games: backgammon, checkers, go, hearts, mahjong, shogi, sudoku, solitaire, xiangqi, and a Scrabble alternative called word. They’re all part of Chess’s new Classic Games platform, which is launching its public beta on Saturday on the web and through a new app for iOS and Android.
Chess.com’s next move is a new hub for classic games, from mahjong to sudoku
AI changed the game at Chess.com, helping it expand to 11 other classics this year.
“Our cofounders have had many people come up to them and say, ‘Hey, I run a mahjong night on Wednesdays’ or ‘I go to this local bar in Chicago with like five people, and we love playing go, but we lack a Chess.com,’” chief growth officer Albert Cheng says in an interview with The Verge. “The way that Chess.com has grown this community of almost 300 million members has not really happened for a lot of these other types of classic games.”
Classic Games is aimed at filling that gap. Some of the new games, like shoji or xiangqi, are strategy games similar to chess while others are further afield, like sudoku, solitaire, and word. The Classic team chose the new games through “a mix of community feedback, market research, and then just our own confidence in our ability to serve that game well,” Cheng says. It’s focused on classics that “have some sort of lifelong journey of learning and a community.”
Classic Games will feel familiar if you’ve ever played a match on Chess.com. Each game has lessons, leaderboards, and a rating system. Multiplayer games like checkers or mahjong have options for matches against other players or bots, and they use the same bot characters that Chess.com has. (Martin remains the lowest-rated bot across the board, whether it’s on Chess, Gambit, or Classic.) Not all of the games have the same play modes — word and mahjong have puzzles like chess, while sudoku has a set of daily grids and solitaire has daily deals.
The expansion hasn’t put Chess.com itself on the back burner, according to Cheng. If anything, it’s never been better. “Chess is more and more so in the public zeitgeist than I’ve ever seen it, frankly, during my time here,” Cheng says. “Our daily active users are higher than they’ve ever been during the company’s history.” He declined to share exactly how many daily users Chess.com currently has but said the site is “doing amazingly well.”
So, while the company is expanding beyond its domain name, chess remains its primary focus. “The amount of folks that are fully dedicated toward building new games is less than 1 percent of the company,” according to Cheng.
AI played a key role in helping Chess.com launch 11 new games in a matter of months with a team of only a few people. Earlier this year, Cheng told The Verge his team built Gambit with the help of AI, mainly for coding tasks. He says they used “almost entirely the same approach” for Classic, with AI helping to speed up the coding process again.
“Because these games are built on top of the Chess.com code base and design system and bot characters and rating systems, it’s a huge advantage and allows us to move very quickly alongside AI to bring these types of games to market with a very small team,” Cheng says. “As we create more and more games, the adjacent games that can be created to it just happen much faster because the infrastructure is there, as opposed to standing everything up from scratch.”
AI wasn’t used for Classic Games’ art and design, Cheng says. “The look and feel of it is very carefully crafted by humans, and we’re proud of that,” he says. “The truth is, it really is a blend. It’s a small team of really talented folks that have good product and design judgment, and they’re leveraging AI.”
“We are fortunate in some ways that AI and chess have been intermixed for 30-ish years.”
Chess.com’s comfort with AI may come from the fact that human chess players have now spent decades playing and learning alongside machines. “We are fortunate in some ways that AI and chess have been intermixed for 30-ish years,” Cheng says, calling back to Garry Kasparov’s 1996 chess match against IBM’s Deep Blue supercomputer. “Even before the company was founded 20 years ago, the idea that AI was super powerful at the game of chess was embedded in how the cofounders thought about the company.”
Elsewhere in the games industry, there’s been increasing tension over the use of AI. Cheng says that while Chess.com may be using AI to “accelerate” coding tasks, the creative side of things has become more important. “On the art and the design side, the ratios are shifting a decent amount, where we’re hiring more of those folks,” he says, adding that the company has “shipped a lot more major features in Chess.com than in previous years” using what they’ve learned from Classic Games’ faster development process.
Chess.com might not be done growing its library of games, either. Cheng said it will likely expand to “a lot more” games in the future.

items.text:
My Monitor Was Cutting My Download Speed by 75%
Somehow I am one of those few very lucky people to have the opportunity of owning a 2.5 gig symmetrical line for my internet. But one day, when I wanted to brag to my equally nerdy friends, shock and horror: 600 Mbps down? Luckily my upload speed was still 2.4 Gbps, so I didn’t lose all my bragging rights, but that’s weird, right? If anything, you’d expect the opposite!
My ISP is pretty cool. It’s run by this one guy (Hey Keith!), and I know I can always message them and they respond promptly, as they did this time. We tried to run through a few debugging steps, they checked on their end, and everything was normal. I tried my work laptop too, same speed.
I didn’t have time for debugging, because I needed to travel 2000 km to the other side of the continent for a family emergency.
But as soon as I got back, I got curious again. What could it be? In retrospect, I now know when it started: when I moved all my connections onto my Studio Display XDR. I wanted to have a one-cable setup, and the monitor offered me that. I’ve had it for half a year now, and I don’t think I’ve ever run a speed test through it. 600 Mbps was more than fast enough for me to never realise I wasn’t getting three quarters of the speed I was paying for 🤦
The setup#
- MacBook Pro M3 Pro
- 2026 Studio Display XDR, with everything plugged into it so switching laptops is one cable
- UGREEN USB-C to 2.5G Ethernet adapter, plugged into the display
- UniFi Dream Router 7, the same one from my WiFi 7 debugging post
What I thought was interesting#
Pings to other wired computers during a download would fail 10% of the time over Ethernet through the adapter plugged into my screen, and 0% of the time over Wi-Fi. What made it stranger was that there were no dropped frame errors in macOS’s logs at all. This was the big hint for me: the adapter was dropping them before the computer could know.
I then plugged the adapter straight into my Mac instead of the monitor, and ran an iperf3 server on my UDR 7: 2.3 Gbps. So the cable, the router and the adapter are all fine? What about fast.com? Perfect speeds there too! 2.2 down and 2.3 up when connected straight in. As soon as I connected it to the display, it was back to 600 down again.
So it’s the display, right? Well, I would find out: sort of yes, sort of no, which is why I wanted to write this blog post. I couldn’t find anything online explaining the exact cause, and it’s quite a cool reason.
The driver and flow control#
The adapter uses a Realtek RTL8156B, which on macOS binds to Apple’s generic USB networking driver. But Realtek ship their own driver on their website, so I thought I’d give that a go! I installed it and, to my surprise, it almost doubled the download speed to 1.1 Gbps, but that was still nowhere close to 2.5. First hint that it couldn’t just be the monitor’s fault.
Then I tried flow control. I had never truly looked into this before, and I think it’s quite neat to know about if you were also ignorant of it like me. Basically, when a device receives Ethernet frames it can’t keep up with, it just drops them. With flow control (it’s something your router or switch has to support), it can send the sender a “pause” frame, and the sender then buffers the data on its side, instead of the receiver (the adapter in this case) on its side. I turned it on in my UniFi console and guess what, download jumped to around 2 Gbps, with upload still at full speed! Yay! Well, not so fast…
I don’t like it always being on, because it can add latency to other systems like my gaming PC. Can you work around it? For sure, you can disable it on those computers, but it’s janky, and it’s another thing I need to remember when my Sauerbraten game starts lagging. I need fewer things to remember, considering I am 30 in a couple of months. My memory is not what it used to be.
But the upload was always fine#
Yeah, isn’t that weird? First of all, it looks like the port can indeed do 2.5 in both directions. I already knew that, because I get much more than that from my external SSD through the monitor’s Thunderbolt port. So the issue is not the monitor again? But it has to be!
Well, I had another idea. How about I connect to my Linux box, which is also on 2.5, and send perfectly smooth UDP traffic at a fixed rate with flow control off? Then I can check the chip’s own counter of dropped frames:
So basically no drops whatsoever when connected straight to my Mac, but loads of drops after about 168k frames per second (roughly 2 Gbps). Remember that number. That number comes from the adapter’s own counters: however much I sent, the number of frames it managed to hand over to the Mac each second flattened out at about 168,000, and everything above that was dropped.
Why did this not happen on my SSD? What was the only difference I could find? Bursts!
When the Mac reads data from a USB 3 device, the device sends some packets, then has to wait for the Mac to say “lgtm, send more!”. The SSD enclosure sends 16 packets before needing a go-ahead message back. The RTL8156B in my Ethernet adapter sends 4.
Here is a diagram of my best understanding of why this is an issue. I made this diagram 100 times, and I think I can probably improve it more, but if it helps you understand the issue, I have done my job.
As you can see, the speed of packets coming into the adapter is 2.5 Gbps. That’s what the router pushes in. The speed going out is around 2 Gbps. The reason is that if you add up the average time it takes to get the go-ahead through my monitor’s hub, which is around 7.6 µs, to the average time it takes to send 4 KB, around 8.2 µs, you can find what the maximum speed is.
Well, if the speed of the drain from my adapter to my Mac is half a gig slower than the speed of the input, then you can imagine the buffer getting filled more and more until it overflows. Those are dropped packets, which result in a hard backoff when the router resends them, so you drop loads in speed. And

items.text:
[Announce] GnuPG Security Advisory for GPGME (T8557,CVE-2026-129975)
Werner Koch 
    wk at gnupg.org
       
Fri Nov 20 19:01:51 CET 2026
    
    
Hello!
We are pleased to announce the availability of a new GPGME release:
version 2.3.1.  This version fixes a *critical security bug* found in
all prior versions.  We also release a new Gpg4win versions and and
GnuPG Desktop and GnuPG VS-Desktop versions which all make use of GPGME.
Description
===========
By using an OpenPGP key containing a crafted very long user id it is
possible to trigger a double free.  This double free can be used
exfiltrate data from applications by sending for example signed data.
Exploiting this bug to mount an Remote Code Execution attack (RCE) can't
be ruled out.  Thus an immediate update is highly suggested.
Our internal ID is T8557 (https://static.dev.gnupg.org/T8557)
The CVE-id is CVE-2026-129975.
This vulnerability was discovered by Johan Carlsson and we were informed
by GitLab on 2026-11-12.  Initially we set 2026-11-25 for a coordinated
disclosure; due to the new Ruby2Shell bug GitLab had to update earlier
and thus we also disclosed the GPGME bug on 2026-11-20.
The root cause for this bug are two GPGME internal functions to read the
status lines and key listings from gpg.  Initially a buffer of 1024
bytes is allocated which is reallocated if more space is required.  When
reallocating the pointer to the new buffer is used by the function but
it is only assigned back to the context object at the end of the
function.  Thus if the function returns early due to an read error or
other events the context is not updated and keeps the stale pointer to
the freed memory.  Eventually the context is released and the memory
freed a second time.  Due to other allocations in between the common
double free checks of memory allocators may not be triggered.
Impact
======
All software using a GPGME version prior to 2.3.0 either as shared
libary, DLL, or statically linked is affected.  Examples of software
using GPGME are
 - Gpg4win
 - GnuPG Desktop
 - GnuPG VS-Desktop
 - Most mail clients
 - Many XMPP clients
 - Samba
 - Flatpack
Solution
========
Please update your GPGME shared library to version 2.3.1.  If you need a
DLL you may take it from from the updated Gpg4win version.
For statically linked binaries remmeber to build them against GPGME
2.3.1.
If for some reasons GPGME can't be updated, you may patch your GPGME
version using the attached patch which likley applies cleanly even to
very old versions.
There is no need to udpate GPGMEPP or GPGMEQT.
Noteworthy changes in version 2.3.1 (2026-11-19)
================================================
         [compared to version 2.2.0]
 * New constants GPGME_PK_MLKEM, GPGME_PK_MLDSA, and GPGME_PK_DLTHM.
   Add mappings for algos used bei backends.   [rMa85fa49236]
 * Fix a double free in the status line read code.
   [T8557,CVE-2026-129975]
 * Interface changes relative to the 2.2.0 release:
 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 GPGME_PK_DLTHM                NEW.
 GPGME_PK_MLKEM                NEW.
 GPGME_PK_MLDSA                NEW.
 Release-info: https://dev.gnupg.org/T8427
Getting the Software
====================
Please follow the instructions found at <https://gnupg.org/download/> or
read on:
The GPGME source code compressed using BZIP2 and its OpenPGP signature
are available here:
 https://gnupg.org/ftp/gcrypt/gpgme/gpgme-2.3.1.tar.bz2 (1393k)
 https://gnupg.org/ftp/gcrypt/gpgme/gpgme-2.3.1.tar.bz2.sig
A sufficient patch to solve the security bug for older versions is
attached.   Note that version 2.3.0 was never publicly available.
Debian Packages
===============
We also provide Debian style packages for a couple of Debian variants.
See https://repos.gnupg.org/deb/gnupg/trixie/ or use the menu to switch
to other distros/releases.
Windows Installer
=================
A new version of Gpg4win (5.1.2), our full featured Windows installer,
including the fixed version of GPGME, the Kleopatra GUI, and a PDF
reader has also been released.  Head over to https://gpg4win.org/
Checking the Integrity
======================
See https://gnupg.org/download/integrity_check.html
The checksum for gpgme is:
1134a407b50204ee6fb9efaa6e1451c2460e543e  gpgme-2.3.1.tar.bz2
*Thank you all*
   Your GnuPG hackers
p.s.
This is an announcement only mailing list.  Please send replies only to
the gnupg-users at gnupg.org mailing list.

  To guarantee that a downloaded version has not been tampered by

  binary versions.  The keys are also signed by the long term keys of
  their respective owners.  Current releases are signed by one or more

ANC fights to keep control of South Africa's key cities after election setback

items.text:
ANC fights to keep control of South Africa's key cities after election setback
- Published
The party that has dominated South Africa for more than 30 years is in a race against time to secure power-sharing deals in most of the country's cities after a massive drop in its support in this month's local elections.
The African National Congress (ANC) suffered its worst result since it came to power in 1994 when South Africa transitioned from the racist apartheid system to democracy.
It won a majority in just one of the country's nine provinces, Limpopo, down from six in the last elections. It won the most votes in just two of the country's eight cities, compared with six in 2021.
At the national level, the ANC is sharing power with its long-time rival, the Democratic Alliance (DA), but while there is still no official announcement, it appears that ANC party officials do not want to replicate this at the local level.
Parties have until 27 November to negotiate and form local governments.
What happened in the local election?
While the ANC saw a massive decline in its support, it still got more votes than any other party, 31%, down from the 46% in the last local election.
But in the country's economic powerhouse, Gauteng province, which includes Johannesburg and Pretoria, the picture is different. The pro-business DA got the most votes in both cities, as well as the province's other main region, Ekurhuleni.
Nationally, the party got 25% of the vote, up from 22% five years ago.
It also retained its majority in its power base of Cape Town, and got the most votes in Nelson Mandela Bay, where Gqeberha (Port Elizabeth) is located.
The left-leaning uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party, led by former President Jacob Zuma, came third, with 10% of the vote. This is a repeat of its performance in the 2024 national election, when it came in third and became the official opposition after the DA joined the coalition government.
It emerged as the biggest party in KwaZulu-Natal province, which includes the port city of Durban, securing 34% of the vote. However, this leaves it reliant on agreeing a coalition with other parties.
The only party to secure an overall majority in a city was the DA in Cape Town.
Why is the ANC apparently choosing smaller parties over the DA?
The DA and ANC have had an uneasy alliance since they entered a coalition, along with eight other political parties, in 2024.
The two, long-standing rivals due to their opposing policies, were forced into an agreement after the ANC lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since the end of apartheid. This became known as the Government of National Unity (GNU).
Despite this, the two parties have continued to disagree on key issues, and both sides have threatened to rip up their power-sharing deal.
Ahead of the local elections, analysts predicted that the two parties could team up at municipal level, mirroring the national arrangement.
The ANC seems to have rejected this, with state broadcaster SABC reporting that most of the party's top leaders see an agreement with the DA as a last resort.
Instead, the party has been courting smaller parties to try and form councils in South Africa's cities.
In Gauteng, numerous reports point to an arrangement between the party and the anti-immigrant ActionSA, which emerged as the third largest party in the province with 17%, leaving it as a potential kingmaker.
The DA has also been trying to reach arrangements with smaller parties, and the ANC, but looks set to assume the opposition benches at least in Gauteng.
ActionSA is unlikely to work with the DA as they cannot agree on the mayoral candidates in Johannesburg and Pretoria.
Does this signal a breakdown in the relationship between the ANC and DA nationally?
It's too early to tell. Neither the ANC nor DA have spoken publicly about the future of their arrangement on a national level amid the ongoing coalition talks but the ANC's reluctance to partner with the DA in key cities points to continued strain between the two.
While the GNU has remained intact since it was formed in 2024, there have been those in the ANC who have been angered by what they view as the DA's dual role as opposition and partner in the coalition government and have pushed for the arrangement to end.
A party insider told the Daily Maverick on Sunday that a nationwide agreement to work with the DA at municipal level "was overwhelmingly rejected" at a meeting held by ANC members.
While some experts predict that the DA may have to consider its position in the coalition government given the ANC's stance, political analyst Andre Duvenhage told the BBC there was a possibility that "a lot of asymmetrical coalitions" could emerge - parties working together in one area and being in opposition elsewhere.
Another political analyst, Sandile Swana, said that any party wanting to leave the GNU over the failure to secure deals locally would be "[shooting] yourself in the foot".
Would coalition governments improve services?
This is what voters want.
The decline in the ANC's support was seen as being mainly due to high levels of corruption and a loss of confidence in its ability to provide basic services, such as electricity, water and rubbish collection.
While some attribute the increase backing for the DA to its record of competent management in municipalities under its control, some have accused it of neglecting poorer areas and townships.
But the experience of coalition governments over the past 10 years does not inspire much confidence that things will improve.
Half of the country's cities have been governed through power-sharing agreements since 2016 and these types of arrangements have often been viewed as unstable and chaotic.
As agreements collapse and new ones are forged, the delivery of basic services has often been affected.
This has been particularly evident in Gauteng, where governance in all three cities has come under scrutiny in recent years partly because of unstable governments.

NINLIVE
The Nine Inch Nails live archive
Explore shows, download recordings, stream audio, and follow the tape trail across every era. Fan run, not affiliated with the band.
From the archive
The Future Is Here - ninlive Streaming 1988-2026
Besides a database driven site. The second most requested feature for ninlive is streaming capability. The future is now. TJ has been working hard behind the scenes to make it happen. You are now able to stream all of your favorite NIN live recordings from 1988-2026. I can't believe how far the site has come in the last year. Some truly incredible work. Login with your discord account and you can save your favorite recordings to stream and keep your faves organized. As always, feedback is always welcome. Reach out via email if you have comments/suggestions about it.
I am currently adding all of the ticket stubs, setlist scans, passes that I have for each show. Please get in contact if you have anything to contribute. I am also looking for photos from past shows. If you are a photographer and would like to contribute some highlights, I'd love to add them to the archive with a link directed to your site of choice.
Other than that. A few tapes trickling in and I do have some that I am slowly working on. None that are insane upgrades. But would need some work and comparison of previous versions. Notably, I have a 1st gen cassette of the 07/12/1991 NOLA Tipitina's show that sounds killer. I recently transferred the elusive collection of acc123456 and have a queue of VHS/Cassette transfers to check over. I also just finished a 200 DAT tape project for a fellow taper out of NYC. The transfer backlog is clear, for the first time in a while. So if you need anything transferred, or have some old NIN hanging around that isn't on the archive. Email us!

items.title: Pill to treat pancreatic cancer hailed as 'biggest breakthrough in decades'
items.summary:
A pill that can shrink and potentially eliminate pancreas tumours is being hailed as the biggest breakthrough treatment for the cancer in decades.
In one in 12 of the patients given the drug, daraxonrasib, during a trial, the cancer became undetectable, and the tumours stopped growing in almost all
items.text:
A pill that can shrink and potentially eliminate pancreas tumours is being hailed as the biggest breakthrough treatment for the cancer in decades.
In one in 12 of the patients given the drug, daraxonrasib, during a trial, the cancer became undetectable, and the tumours stopped growing in almost all of the 61 patients. The trial participants had recently been diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body.
Though doctors have said the pill cannot yet be considered a cure, and they do not know how long it can keep the disease at bay, they have said it is encouraging news because it appears it will offer patients more time, even if it does not cause full remission.
Half of all people diagnosed with pancreatic cancer die within three months, and only about 3% of patients survive for five years when the disease spreads to other organs. It has the lowest survival rate of all common cancers in the UK and has a similarly poor prognosis globally.
Patients were followed for a year and a half during the trial on average and some did not see the cancer return during this period. Longer studies will be conducted to see if any of the cancers can be put into remission. During the trial, tumours stopped growing in 90% of patients, just over 60% of patients had their tumours shrink or disappear, and for about 8% of patients tumours became undetectable on CT scans.
A year after starting treatment, 76.6% of patients were alive; usually 40-45% of patients given chemotherapy alone survive a year.
Dr Wungki Park, a gastrointestinal medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, who presented the findings, said “this is the closest to cure”, adding that he had never seen so many tumours disappear in patients whose cancer had spread.
He presented the findings at the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium on Molecular Targets and Cancer Therapeutics in Barcelona. “We are beginning to see not only a higher percentage of tumour response rates, but also deeper responses and a near doubling in the duration of disease control, which may eventually translate into longer survival,” he said.
“The median follow-up is 18 months. Just imagine, in an average of 18 months your disease just disappears on the CT scan … that’s closest to complete remission … it’s incredible.”
Daraxonrasib is a KRAS inhibitor treatment, which works by locking on to and shutting off certain mutations found in most pancreatic cancers. These mutations drive tumour growth.
There are hopes the treatment could work for dozens of other cancers because they can have similar mutations.
Michelle Mitchell, Cancer Research UK’s chief executive, said more research was needed, but added: “This is the biggest leap forward we’ve seen in decades for pancreatic cancer patients and could offer real hope to people facing one of the deadliest and most difficult-to-treat cancers.
“These results raise the exciting possibility that this breakthrough could eventually pave the way for treating other cancers that carry Kras gene mutations. More trials are now needed before this treatment can be assessed for use on the NHS and despite this advance, pancreatic cancer survival is still very low.”

items.text:
It’s been a little bit quiet around these parts; sorry about that. I’ve been really busy for the past fifteen months with a major project that I am finally ready to formally release. So I’d like to talk about that project, and also a potted history of AI and Emacs.
It’s called DreamCoder, an AI coding harness that is very different from the ones you’re probably familiar with already.
I installed Claude Code a few days after its first release some time in May 2025. I put some coins in the slot machine and I put it to work building a complex piece of enterprise middleware I’d built several times in my career. Wow.. watching this thing chomp its way through the project with that chaotic, early Sonnet energy. It was far, far from perfect; it required a lot of human steering, input and correction, but the speed advantage was undeniable, and seeing it jump between disparate programming languages, frameworks and theoretical and practical programming from one turn to the next was just such a sight to behold.
One thing that struck me with Claude Code is that it was the first terminal application I’d used in a long time. I found it an odd choice for a coding agent; then everyone else copied them and made their own terminal coding agents.
Why on earth do I have to stare at a shoe rack-sized terminal window to do this? Sure there are GUI versions also; but the terminal interface remains the primary modality for most of these tools. Most GUIs, and most harnesses now have them also, are second-class citizens. And they all look the same. A boring sidebar with chat headings and a chat pane is what most of them look like.
But a serious coder needs more than that. Even a casual user will bristle when they try to copy and paste multi-line text in a terminal.
So in May 2025 I decreed that I would build a better harness, and surely now that I have AI this should not take more than 2 or 3 months to build.
And so, after 15 months of work, and endless UI and backend iterations, culminating in a successful beta test, I am now ready to release DreamCoder, which is I think the acme of what a coding harness should be.
Before I get into the meat and potatoes of all of that, I want to talk about AI history and Emacs’s role in it.
Let’s roll back time to the 1950s.
Past
Emacs and LISP, if you did not know, both have a special place in the annals of AI history.
John McCarthy was an AI researcher at MIT, and in the 1950s he set out to create the Advice Taker, a piece of software that envelops a framework for what a basic human should know that he called commonsense reasoning using “mathematical logic”. His postulation was that if we can express with symbolic precision all the aspects of what constitutes humanity like ordinary facts about life, that we can set in motion the rudiments of AI.
In the 50s there was little in the way of computer software that could do this. To formalize such a system you need a lot of data, rigorously formatted, and a method of manipulating the data. The data and code itself may intertwine recursively, and so an ordinary programming language would not work.
To help him achieve this, McCarthy created the LISt Processing (LISP) language made up of two facets: M-expressions, a functional language in the vein of Algol; and S-expressions, designed for symbolic data representation, and never intended as a method of writing code. S-expressions were dolled up with parentheses. M-expressions meanwhile used square brackets to visually separate the two. Uniquely, the language specification had an eval feature that would prove that the language is also a universal Turing machine… if only McCarthy had the means to do so. It was theoretical because McCarthy lacked, in time, staff and money, what he needed build this recursive evaluator that can take as input its own world state and evaluate it alongside new expressions, a fact made even more apparent by the sheer complexity of his M-expression language and the limited resources he had at the time.
Steve Russell who worked with him proved him wrong the way most young people do: by just doing it. Russell wrote the first LISP Interpreter with a working eval function, but M-expressions got sidelined; the imperative, procedural nature of programming got squished into S-expressions instead. They had to hand roll the language on paper then punch it into cards and then batch run them. Eliding M-expressions was a simple matter of pragmatism. And so LISP was born. And through several accidents of history, M-expressions never gained traction. M-expressions live on in Wolfram’s Mathematica, but few other places.
Much later, McCarthy eventually conceded that,
“One can even conjecture that LISP owes its survival specifically to the fact that its programs are lists, which everyone, including me, has regarded as a disadvantage.”
S-expressions were always intended as the storage format with a bridge language to manipulate them. But by pushing evaluation into the same symbolic representation format as the data, we have what we call LISP today. That is why LISP is so unique. Consider a simple calculator. (+ 2 2) can simultaneously represent an expression that we want to compute, two plus two, or perhaps a ledger of record of a calculation we have already done.
McCarthy never built the Advice Taker in its purest form. He and his team ran into many philosophical, mathematical and computational walls that kept them occupied for a long time.
The idea behind the Advice Taker was simple. If you want to go somewhere in your car, you can symbolically express this by building a chain of narrative facts – kinda like a flowchart, but as small snippets of rules and facts, not as one grand design.
The system would automatically resolve ambiguities, and all the logician had to do was capture the microcosm of the world he wished to represent:
(at me home)
(walkable home car)
(walkable home driveway)
(drivable car shop)
And so on. If you’re a student of Computer Science you’ll see echoes of

items.text:
The stochastic parrots have apparently proved the Riemann Hypothesis
“… it is very probable that all roots are real. Of course one would wish for a rigorous proof here; I have for the time being, after some fleeting vain attempts, provisionally put aside the search for this, as it appears dispensable for the immediate objective of my investigation.” –Bernhard Riemann, 1859
[Update: According to “Poe’s Law,” there is no irony or sarcasm on the Internet so obvious that it won’t fly over countless people’s heads. In line with that, lots of people on social media are now saying variants of “how dare Scott Aaronson call LLMs ‘stochastic parrots,’ that demeaning and trivializing term from 2021? Doesn’t he understand that these so-called ‘stochastic parrots’ just proved the Riemann Hypothesis?” ROFL.]
I’m in California to visit Oratomic and then Inkhaven. I woke up this morning to the news that Levent Alpöge says that he’s gotten Anthropic models to prove the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, producing 17.4 million (!!) lines of Lean code.
At a dinner last night, someone asked me “so, how much longer until an AI proves the Riemann Hypothesis? Still several more years?” I replied, don’t be sure of such things anymore. After all, AI has already proved that the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function are at most 3/8 away from the critical line (Quanta just published its article on that breakthrough yesterday!), and that already carries most of the implications for number theory that a full proof of RH would have. So who the hell knows what else is possible, and how quickly?
For those tuning in from home, the Riemann Hypothesis says (in its easiest-to-understand version) that the number of prime numbers from 1 to n is very close to what it would be if each integer x>1 had an independent 1/ln(x) probability of being prime, up to a standard statistical error term that never exceeds Õ(√n). While we’ve known since 1896 that the number of primes from 1 to n is asymptotic to n/ln(n) (that’s the famous Prime Number Theorem), you could’ve imagined the deviations being much larger.
David Hilbert famously said, “If I were to awaken after having slept for a thousand years, my first question would be: Has the Riemann Hypothesis been proven?” Meanwhile G. H. Hardy, on a ship that he feared might sink, sent his colleagues a telegram claiming to have proven RH, so that if the worst came to pass, at least the world might believe that a proof sank with him.
Many will of course question whether the proof announced today will stand. They’ll point out that, despite how heavily the world is now “lean-ing” on it, the Lean formal verification system still has issues, from kernel bugs (which have, in the past, allowed proofs of 0=1) to uncertain soundness of the underlying type theory. In my view, these issues can and should urgently be fixed! Until they are, a sufficiently motivated AI could almost certainly exploit them to prove a false statement!
All the same, I see zero indications that that’s happening right now. I note that, so far, not one of the AI results with Lean certificates has needed to be retracted (while several without Lean certificates have needed to be). So I’m not 100% sure, but my bet is that the proof will stand.
Mathematicians of course won’t be satisfied with 17 million lines of Lean. They’ll be satisfied when, and only when, they’re able to explain and distill and reconstruct the ideas for themselves. And that will probably take years, since human mathematicians move only at biological speeds. And while they’re working on it, how many more such wonders will there be, in this age of wonders and terrors?
My 9-year-old son, informed that RH was proved, replied that he’s not even surprised at this point. Maybe you need to have come of age in the human math era to be surprised by such things.
The P=?NP problem now moves firmly into place as the Final Boss of the Math We’ve Cared About, the position I always thought it should occupy. But for how much longer? For how much longer will anything last that we currently take for granted?
It was only a couple days ago that my wife and I had the following conversation:
Dana: I turned off the irrigation, yet somehow water in our house is still leaking. We need to…
Me: Look, a lot of the smartest people I know now think that recursive self-improvement and the end of the entire known world are coming in 12-18 months. This leak…
Dana: We should still fix the leak.

items.summary:
Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a stealthy fusion power startup founded by an AI researcher who is taking a different approach to developing a fusion power plant.
The UK-based startup was founded in February, though sources told TechCrunch that the founder, Nantas Nardelli, has b
items.text:
Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a stealthy fusion power startup founded by an AI researcher who is taking a different approach to developing a fusion power plant.
The UK-based startup was founded in February, though sources told TechCrunch that the founder, Nantas Nardelli, has been working on the idea for longer. The people asked not to be identified because the information isn’t public. Bloomberg first reported Ek’s backing of Europa Fusion.
Nardelli has extensive experience in the AI world, having previously worked at Google DeepMind, Facebook AI Research, and Microsoft Research Cambridge. Recently, he was head of machine learning at Pacific Fusion, the fusion power startup based in Fremont, California.
Pacific Fusion recently broke ground on a demonstration facility in New Mexico. Like most fusion startups of its size, Pacific Fusion leans heavily on physical devices to test its theories and improve its simulations.
Nardelli apparently didn’t agree with the focus on hardware, instead thinking that fusion startups should invest in a more simulation- and data-heavy approach, a source familiar with his thinking told TechCrunch.
Like Pacific Fusion, Europa Fusion will pursue a pulsed-power approach to fusion. Pulsed-power reactors use massive, perfectly timed surges of electrical current to compress fuel targets until the atoms inside fuse and release energy.
Fusion power has the potential to be a significant energy source in the coming decades, but to date, no one has built a power plant capable of supplying electricity to the grid. If fusion power becomes commercially viable, though, it could possibly be a significant source of carbon-free power that draws on nearly limitless fuel supplies. The technology also has the potential to alleviating concerns about AI’s energy consumption.
Fusion’s ability to generate electricity without exacerbating climate change apparently drove Nardelli’s pivot from AI.
“My original background is in electronics and control engineering,” he wrote on his website. “I used to build robots for a living. One day I’ll be back to that, but it’s time to fix climate change for good.”

items.text:
Ghanaian boy killed in US 'deserved so much better', says New York Mayor Mamdani
- Published
A 15-year-old Ghanaian boy who was killed in the US last month was remembered as a hard-working student with dreams of becoming a doctor, as his father, New York City's mayor and civil rights leaders gave eulogies during his funeral on Friday.
Javits Frimpong was shot and killed while walking to school in the Bronx. His death has sparked outrage in both Ghana and the US, and reignited debates about gun violence in America.
"Javits deserved so much better and so do every single one of you," Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. "Though he was only a New Yorker for a short time, New York City will forever be proud to call Javits one of our own."
Frimpong moved to the US about a year before the shooting.
"I worked hard to bring you from Ghana to America because I wanted you to have opportunities, a better future, and a chance to achieve everything that you dreamed of," his father, Thomas Frimpong, said.
His mother was granted an emergency visa from Ghana to mourn her son at Friday's funeral service, following Mamdani's lobbying of President Donald Trump earlier this month.
Frimpong was chased down and shot on 29 October. He was taken to a local hospital, where he was pronounced dead.
Police have said three teenage boys were involved in the shooting. A 17-year-old has been arrested and charged with murder, and will be tried as an adult. Police are still searching for the other two.
"Gun violence is never the answer," Ben Crump, an attorney representing the family, said at the funeral as he vowed to seek justice for Frimpong.
Ghana's government has condemned the killing and said it would follow the case closely to ensure justice was achieved.
It has urged US authorities to conduct a thorough investigation and said it was ready to provide legal and consular support to ensure the perpetrators were brought to justice.

items.summary:
It’s a big week for Levent Alpöge: The mathematician saw his employer, Anthropic, become the first publicly-traded frontier AI lab. He also appears to have solved one of the most important problems in mathematics.
“The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote in an essay announcing his findings and des
items.text:
It’s a big week for Levent Alpöge: The mathematician saw his employer, Anthropic, become the first publicly-traded frontier AI lab. He also appears to have solved one of the most important problems in mathematics.
“The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote in an essay announcing his findings and describing how he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last Sunday night to ask how to announce that he had found a Lean-compilable solution to the Riemann Hypothesis, which dates back to 1859 and is among the Millennium Prize math problems.
The Hypothesis conjectures that there is a hidden structure underlying the appearance of prime numbers. If the claimed result holds true, we’re entering sublime-mysteries-of-the-universe territory.
Maybe the best way to understand how exciting this is to the mathematics community is to watch the experts puzzling through the result in a chat on Zulip. Mathematicians like Chris Birbeck, a number theorist at the University of East Anglia, are posting thoughts like this …
The cohomology bound is proved by what looks like an automorphy-lifting argument. It genuinely uses the existence of Galois representations attached to regular algebraic, polarized cuspidal automorphic representations of GL_n over CM fields, along with base change, Jacquet–Shalika, Clozel’s purity, Bernstein–Zelevinsky, the main theorem of CM, Deligne–Ribet and more.
For my part, I tapped out of mathematics at college calculus, so I can’t help decode exactly what that means.
But that comment was followed by twenty readers reacting 🤯.
It will be a while before the mathematics community feels like it has a handle on the proof, but most appear confident that the formalized Lean result will hold. Lean is an an open-source language that essentially helps verify mathematical proofs.
Alpöge appeared in his essay to feel a bit guilty about releasing the proof without a truly human-intelligible explanation, but his obsession with the problem since childhood made him feel he “could not live” if he waited to release the finding.
Alpöge described a “stream-of-consciousness jaunt through the experience of finding all the pieces of the argument through incredible confusion with Claude” with more than a hint of AI euphoria, describing how the model “flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.”
However, for all that action to mean anything, we’ll have to wait for humans to be able to understand the result and explain it to each other, something Alpöge has committed to pursue.
Alpöge and a collaborator, NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, also released another important proof related to the Navier-Stokes equations, problems that helped kick off the race between frontier labs and mathematicians to solve outstanding problems this summer.
Meanwhile, Ravi Vakil, a Stanford professor and the president of the American Mathematics Association, posted a proof of the General Riemann Hypothesis written by Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo, noting that “it is all human, with no AI. The hope was to bring Alessandro to Stanford for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current draft.”
In a brief introduction his proof, which he said is the result of twelve years of work, Masullo wrote that “if any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this: we are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere.”

While
items.text:
President Donald Trump promised to put a “tremendous tax” on companies that build data centers outside of the US, even as states and cities around the country are placing restrictions on new applications to build them.
Trump threatens ‘tremendous tax’ for moving AI data centers outside the US
While policymakers across the country are putting new restrictions on the data center buildout, Trump is making threats.
“We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country,” Trump said at a press conference Friday following his summit with China President Xi Jinping and Russia President Vladimir Putin. “They allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country. It’s where we started going behind.” Should the US allow data centers to be built outside of the country, Trump warned, “China will take them all.”
Trump didn’t share many details behind the plan, and apparently was floating the proposal publicly for the first time. “I don’t know if that’s a breaking story. But I haven’t even said that to my people,” Trump said, flanked by Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. “But I’m telling them now. They’re here. Many of them are here.”
Trump’s promise could be difficult to fulfill with a new Democratic majority Congress being sworn in within a couple of months. Even members of his own party recognize that the data center buildout has become an unpopular issue across the board. With states installing moratoriums and new restrictions on data center proposals, companies may be forced to look outside of the country, but Trump’s threat is an attempt to make that a less attractive alternative.
Here’s a transcript of the key part of Trump’s remarks:
Whoever wins SI wins. And you ought to take advantage of the data centers. Make them pay you. Make them pay your community. But take advantage. Don’t shut them off. And there’s always somebody else in this country. But if it’s not this country, there’s somebody else outside.
We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country. We’re not going to allow that to happen. You know, they allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country. It’s where we started going behind.
So I just, I don’t know if that’s a breaking story. But I haven’t even said that to my people, but I’m telling them now. They’re here. Many of them are here. And we’re not going to allow companies to build data centers in other countries. If they do that, they can, but we’re going to put a tremendous tax on them.

Monitoring new customers is the most important part of running a business, so he is absolutely right in doin
items.text:
Yesterday, I was debugging a performance problem with our Google Forms addon. It turned out my colleague had vibe coded the logging part, so that he could monitor the new installs every week. Monitoring new customers is the most important part of running a business, so he is absolutely right in doing that. Except, he was logging the user’s email and Google has severely restricted how much detail you can get about the user since last December. So, AI had written a series of try/catch statements:
- First, try to get the email if the user gave consent to share it during installation.
- If it fails, it would try to fetch his user ID.
- If that fails, it would log an error saying the user has installed, but we don’t know his email or user ID.
All of these are one line of code, but internally each of these makes multiple API calls to Google servers. Since logging was the first line to execute after installation, the welcome screen took 15 seconds to load.
What is the right code for this?
If you are a senior developer or architect who understands the number of API calls behind each method, you would have:
- Logged just the timestamp of the install instead of trying to fetch the email or user ID, and told the marketing team they won’t be able to send the follow-up email based on installation alone.
- Or, if marketing wants the user’s email on install, you would have shown the welcome screen first and logged the email or user ID asynchronously from the browser, while the user is looking at the welcome screen. But calling your server from the addon’s welcome screen might require your server to bypass security and log an unauthenticated payload.
In other words, your job as an architect is to push back on requirements that can slow down the app. Or, find a way to work around the performance and security issues by making it async or accepting a reasonable hack.
Why AI won’t push back
AI is great at writing code. But it doesn’t know if you are launching the app or have millions of users, which it needs to make the right architecture call to log a timestamp vs email. It is also sycophantic and tries to execute your requirements exactly without pushing back, which means you end up with a slow app that takes 15 seconds to load a static welcome screen.
Essentially, if you generate code by specifying your requirements instead of specifying your architecture, AI will decide the architecture on your behalf. It is so paranoid about security that it will never write code to accept an unauthenticated payload. Even if you write it yourself, it will rewrite it into an authenticated payload and screw up performance or force users to sign in again on your app.
Your new job is to architect
AI coding tools are tuned to implement your functional requirements and two non-functional requirements, i.e. security and backward compatibility to avoid breaking your app. This invariably leads to:
- Architecture that trades off performance for security and slows down the app.
- Multiple versions of datamodel design with redundant tables, columns and code.
That means you define the architecture, design the datamodel first and ask AI to code within that constraint. Every time you give a requirement that changes your architecture or design, coding tools have to ask you before changing it, instead of changing it on their own. You have to tell it when it needs to be backward compatible, so it’s ok to keep multiple versions of logic or database tables, and when to delete the old logic and tables and keep a single version for maintainability.
If you are an architect who is used to designing the datamodel, delegating the implementation to developers and then reviewing their code to see if they have implemented it correctly, this should be natural to you. But the problem is that today we have taken developers who were great at coding and moved them into an architect’s job. They see that the job they love, i.e. coding, is now completely done by AI. But nobody has told them about the new job of pushing back on requirements, designing the datamodel, constraining AI to their architecture and reviewing that it falls in line. This is the reason for all the confusion and hate among developers about vibe coding.
Your future as developer
In our case, the right fix is simple. Log the timestamp, show the welcome screen first and tell marketing what they can’t get on install. But AI will never make that call for you, because it doesn’t know your users and it won’t push back on your requirements. That is the architect’s job. If you are a developer, the coding job is going away. But it doesn’t mean your job is going away. Non-developers who don’t understand architecture and design will end up with bad performance and unmaintainable database tables. So, stop missing the coding and become an architect. Learn to push back on requirements, design the datamodel, constrain AI to it and review the code the way an architect reviews a developer’s code. You got promoted. Nobody told you, so I am telling you.
